items.text: משנת הפתיחה: החייבים והפטורים בראייה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Obligation and Exemption from Re'iyah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists all who are obligated in the pilgrimage appearance, then lists exemptions: deaf-mute, imbecile, minor, tumtum, androgyne, women, unemancipated slaves, the lame, blind, sick, elderly, and those unable to walk. It then defines a minor according to Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, and records their dispute about the value of the olah and shelamim offerings.
items.desc: המשנה מונה את כל החייבים במצוות ראייה, ואת הפטורים: חרש שוטה וקטן, טומטום ואנדרוגינוס, נשים ועבדים, חיגר סומא חולה זקן ומי שאינו יכול לעלות ברגליו. לאחר מכן מגדירה המשנה את גיל הקטן לפי בית שמאי ובית הלל, ומביאה מחלוקת נוספת בין בית שמאי לבית הלל בדבר שיעור קרבנות הראייה והחגיגה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that all are obligated in the pilgrimage appearance (ראייה), then lists the exemptions: deaf-mute, imbecile, minor, tumtum, androgyne, women, unemancipated slaves, the lame, blind, sick, elderly, and those unable to walk.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת במצוות הראייה ומונה את הפטורים ממנה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks: who is considered a minor for exemption, and Beit Shammai answers: one who cannot ride on his father's shoulders and ascend from Jerusalem to the Temple Mount.
sub.desc: בית שמאי ובית הלל נחלקים בהגדרת קטן הפטור מהראייה.

sub.desc_en: Beit Hillel responds: a minor is one who cannot hold his father's hand and ascend from Jerusalem to the Temple Mount, citing the verse 'שלוש רגלים' (three pilgrimage festivals).
sub.desc: בית שמאי ובית הלל נחלקים בשיעורי קרבנות הראייה והחגיגה.

sub.text_en: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah records the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the minimum value of the עולה (burnt offering) and the חגיגה (festival peace offering): Beit Shammai says the עולה requires two silver coins and the חגיגה one ma'ah, while Beit Hillel reverses the amounts.
sub.desc: בית שמאי ובית הלל נחלקים בשיעורי קרבנות הראייה והחגיגה.

items.text: גמרא: דורשת את המילה 'הכל'
items.text_en: Gemara's First Question: What does 'הכל' Include?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'הכל' (all) in the Mishnah comes to include. It first suggests it includes a half-slave half-free man. Then it notes that according to Ravina, who exempts such a person, 'הכל' must include a cripple on the first day who became healed on the second day.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה באה המילה 'הכל' לרבות במשנה. תשובה ראשונה: לרבות מי שחציו עבד וחציו בן חורין. אך לרבינא שפוטר אותו, התשובה היא: לרבות חיגר ביום ראשון ונתפשט ביום שני.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what does the word 'הכל' (all) in the Mishnah come to include, and answers: it includes a half-slave half-free person.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה בא לרבות 'הכל' במשנה, ועונה: לרבות מי שחציו עבד וחציו בן חורין.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects that a half-slave half-free person is exempt from ראיה (pilgrimage appearance), so the word 'הכל' must come to include a person who was lame on the first day of the festival and became healthy on the second day.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה בא לרבות 'הכל' במשנה, ועונה: לרבות מי שחציו עבד וחציו בן חורין.

items.text: קושיה על התשובה לפי שיטת 'תשלומין דראשון'
items.text_en: Second Answer: Including a One-Eyed Person
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous answer works only for one who holds that all days are substitutes for each other. For one who holds that all days are substitutes for the first day, 'הכל' must include a one-eyed person.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: התשובה של חיגר ביום ראשון ונתפשט ביום שני מתאימה רק למי שאומר שכל הימים תשלומין זה לזה. אך למי שאומר שכולם תשלומין דראשון, מה באה 'הכל' לרבות? תשובה: לרבות סומא באחת מעיניו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this works according to the opinion that all days are complementary to each other, but asks: according to the opinion that all days are only make-up for the first day, what does 'הכל' come to include?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: לפי הדעה שכל הימים תשלומי ראשון, מה בא 'הכל' לרבות?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: it comes to include a person blind in one eye.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: לפי הדעה שכל הימים תשלומי ראשון, מה בא 'הכל' לרבות?

items.text: ברייתא: סומא באחת מעיניו פטור
items.text_en: Supporting Tanna: One-Eyed Person Exempt
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this answer follows a specific Tanna, as it is taught: Yochanan ben Dahavai says in the name of Rabbi Yehuda that a one-eyed person is exempt from re'iyah, based on the verse 'יראה' 'יראה' — just as one comes to see with two eyes, so one comes to be seen with two eyes.
items.desc: הגמרא מעירה שתשובה זו אינה כתנא יוחנן בן דהבאי בשם רבי יהודה, הסובר שסומא באחת מעיניו פטור מהראייה, שנאמר 'יראה' 'יראה' – כדרך שבא לראות כך בא ליראות, מה לראות בשתי עיניו אף ליראות בשתי עיניו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Yochanan ben Dahavai says in the name of Rabbi Yehuda that a person blind in one eye is exempt from ראיה, based on the verse 'יראה' 'יראה' — just as one comes to see with both eyes, so one must be seen with both eyes.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא בשם יוחנן בן דהבאי ורבי יהודה הפוטרת סומא באחת מעיניו מהראייה, ומסבירה את הדרשה מ'יראה' 'יראה'.

items.text: תירוץ נוסף: שתי משניות שונות
items.text_en: Alternative Resolution: Two Mishnayot
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: the original answer stands, and the difficulty from Ravina is resolved by distinguishing between an earlier and later Mishnah. The earlier Mishnah (Beit Hillel) holds that a half-slave half-free man serves his master one day and himself one day, implying he is obligated, while the later Mishnah exempts him. Beit Shammai then responds to Beit Hillel.
items.desc: הגמרא מציעה תירוץ אחר: לעולם התשובה הראשונה נכונה (לרבות חציו עבד), והקושיה מרבינא מתורצת בכך שיש שתי משניות – משנה ראשונה ומשנה אחרונה. מובאת משנה בפסחים המראה שבית הלל חייבו חציו עבד לעבוד יום אחד לרבו ויום אחד לעצמו, ובית שמאי חולקים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the original answer stands, and Ravina's objection is resolved by distinguishing between the first Mishnah (which obligates a half-slave) and the later Mishnah (which exempts him), citing the Mishnah where Beit Hillel says a half-slave works for his master one day and for himself the next.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהמחלוקת בין רבינא למשנה תלויה בגרסאות שונות של המשנה: כאן כמשנה ראשונה, ושם כמשנה אחרונה.

sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai objects to Beit Hillel's position regarding the half-slave.
sub.desc: בית שמאי משיבים לבית הלל, אך דבריהם נקטעים כאן.

sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai begins their response to Beit Hillel, which continues beyond the section boundary.
sub.desc: בית שמאי משיבים לבית הלל, אך דבריהם נקטעים כאן.

items.text: דין עבד חציו עבד וחציו בן חורין
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling about a half-slave
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a half-slave is obligated in appearance, arguing that if he cannot marry a slavewoman or a free woman, he should be exempt. It resolves that the court forces his master to free him, and Beit Hillel retracted to Beit Shammai's view.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בבעיית עבד חציו עבד וחציו בן חורין, שאינו יכול להינשא לא לשפחה ולא לבת חורין, וכופים את רבו לשחררו משום פריה ורביה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a half-slave is obligated in appearance, arguing that since he cannot marry a slavewoman or a free woman, he should be exempt.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על תקנת חכמים בעבד חציו משוחרר, שפוגעת בעבד עצמו שאינו יכול להינשא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the court forces his master to free him, and Beit Hillel retracted to Beit Shammai's view.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שכופים את רבו לשחררו משום מצוות פריה ורביה, ובית הלל חזרו להורות כבית שמאי.

items.text: Clarifying the definition of a deaf person in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Clarifying the definition of a deaf person in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's 'deaf' refers to one who cannot hear or speak, as taught in a Mishnah. One who can speak but not hear, or hear but not speak, is obligated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's 'deaf' refers to one who cannot hear or speak, and that those who can speak but not hear or hear but not speak are obligated.

items.text: Supporting the definition with a baraita and scriptural proof
items.text_en: Supporting the definition with a baraita and scriptural proof
items.desc_en: A baraita defines a deaf person as one who speaks but cannot hear, and a mute as one who hears but cannot speak, both considered competent. The Gemara proves this from a verse and an alternative folk saying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that defines a deaf person (חֵרֵשׁ) as one who speaks but cannot hear, and a mute (אִלֵּם) as one who hears but cannot speak, both considered fully competent (פִּקְחִין) in all matters.
The Gemara proves the baraita's definitions from a verse (תהלים ל״ח:י״ד) that juxtaposes 'חֵרֵשׁ' with not hearing and 'אִלֵּם' with not opening the mouth.
The Gemara offers an alternative proof from a folk saying that describes a mute as one whose speech has been taken away (אִישְׁתְּקִיל מִילּוּלֵיהּ).

items.text: Resolving a contradiction between sources
items.text_en: Resolving a contradiction between sources
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: one source says such individuals are obligated, another says exempt. Ravina or Rava resolves that the Mishnah is missing text: they are exempt from appearance but obligated in rejoicing, while those who cannot hear or speak, imbeciles, and minors are exempt from both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: one source (the Mishnah's implication) says that a deaf person who can speak but not hear, or hear but not speak, is obligated in appearance and rejoicing, while another baraita explicitly exempts them.

Ravina (or alternatively Rava) resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah is missing text: it originally taught that those who can speak but not hear, or hear but not speak, are exempt from appearance (ראייה) but obligated in rejoicing (שמחה), while those who are completely deaf-mute, imbeciles, and minors are exempt from both.

items.text: תוספתא תומכת
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for the resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that explicitly states: all are obligated in appearance and rejoicing, except for a deaf person who speaks but cannot hear, or hears but cannot speak, who are exempt from appearance but obligated in rejoicing.
items.desc: ברייתא נוספת תומכת בתירוץ: הכל חייבים בראייה ובשמחה, חוץ מחירש שאינו שומע ואינו מדבר, שפטור אף משמחה.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that explicitly supports the resolution: all are obligated in appearance and rejoicing, except for a deaf person who speaks but cannot hear, or hears but cannot speak, who are exempt from appearance.
sub.desc: ברייתא תומכת בתירוץ של רבינא או רבא, ומבדילה בין פטור מראייה לחיוב בשמחה.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that those exempt from re'iyah (appearance) are nonetheless obligated in simchah (joy), except for those who cannot hear or speak, imbeciles, and minors, who are exempt from all commandments. The Gemara asks why they are exempt from re'iyah but obligated in simchah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that those exempt from re'iyah (appearance) are obligated in simchah (joy), except for the deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor, who are exempt from all commandments.
The Gemara asks why these individuals are exempt from re'iyah but obligated in simchah.

items.text: Derivation from Hakhel for re'iyah exemption
items.text_en: Derivation from Hakhel for re'iyah exemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the exemption for re'iyah is derived from a verbal analogy (gezeirah shavah) between 're'iyah' in the pilgrimage context and 're'iyah' in the Hakhel assembly. In Hakhel, the verses exclude those who cannot hear or speak, as derived from 'lishmo'a' and 'lilmod'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the exemption for re'iyah is derived from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 're'iyah' in the pilgrimage context and 're'iyah' in the Hakhel assembly, citing the relevant verses.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the Hakhel verses that those who cannot hear or speak are excluded from the obligation.

items.text: Challenge from deaf-mute scholars and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from deaf-mute scholars and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that a mute cannot learn, citing a story of two deaf-mutes in Rabbi's neighborhood who learned halakhah, Sifra, Sifrei, and all of Talmud. Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi resolve this by reinterpreting the verse as 'lema'an yelammedu' (that they may teach), not 'yilmedu' (that they may learn), thus the exclusion applies only to teaching, not learning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that a mute cannot learn, citing a story of two deaf-mutes in Rabbi's neighborhood who gestured and moved their lips in the study hall.
The story concludes that Rabbi prayed for them and they were healed, revealing they had learned halakhah, Sifra, Sifrei, and all of Talmud.
Mar Zutra resolves the challenge by reinterpreting the verse as 'לְמַעַן יְלַמְּדוּ' (that they may teach), not 'יִלְמְדוּ' (that they may learn).
Rav Ashi confirms the reading 'לְמַעַן יְלַמְּדוּ', arguing that if it were 'יִלְמְדוּ', the exclusion of a mute from learning would be redundant with the exclusion of a deaf person from hearing.

items.text: Rabbi Tanchum on deaf in one ear
items.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum on deaf in one ear
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum rules that a person deaf in one ear is exempt from re'iyah, based on the verse 'be'ozneihem' (in their ears). The Gemara questions the derivation, but concludes that the word 'be'ozneihem' teaches that they must hear, while the general obligation comes from 'neged kol Yisrael'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum rules that a person deaf in one ear is exempt from re'iyah (appearance in the Temple), citing the verse 'be'ozneihem' (in their ears).
The Gemara objects that the word 'be'ozneihem' is needed to teach that the entire people of Israel must hear, but the verse 'neged kol Yisrael' (before all Israel) already teaches that.
The Gemara answers that without 'be'ozneihem', one might think the obligation applies even if they do not hear; the word teaches that they must actually hear.
The Gemara resolves that the requirement to hear is actually derived from the verse 'lema'an yishme'u' (so that they may hear), not from 'be'ozneihem'.

items.text: Rabbi Tanchum on lame in one foot
items.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum on lame in one foot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum rules that a person lame in one foot is exempt from re'iyah, based on the verse 'raglayim' (feet). The Gemara questions this, as 'raglayim' is needed to exclude those with wooden legs, but resolves that the exclusion of the lame comes from the word 'pe'amim' (steps), as taught in a baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum rules that a person lame in one foot is exempt from re'iyah (appearance), citing the verse 'raglayim' (feet).
The Gemara objects that the word 'raglayim' is needed to exclude those with wooden legs (בעלי קבין), not to exempt the lame.
The Gemara resolves that the exclusion of those with wooden legs comes from the word 'pe'amim' (steps), citing a baraita and verses that equate 'pe'amim' with 'raglayim'.

items.text: Rava's homily on the beauty of pilgrimage
items.text_en: Rava's homily on the beauty of pilgrimage
items.desc_en: Rava expounds on the verse 'Mah yafu fe'amayich bane'alim bat nadiv', interpreting it as praise for the feet of Israel when they ascend for the pilgrimage festival, and explaining 'bat nadiv' as the daughter of Abraham, who is called a noble (nadiv).

sub.desc_en: Rava expounds on the verse 'Mah yafu fe'amayich bane'alim bat nadiv', interpreting it as praise for Israel's feet when ascending for the pilgrimage, and explaining 'bat nadiv' as the daughter of Abraham, who is called a noble (nadiv).

items.text: Rav Kahana's homily on the empty pit
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's homily on the empty pit
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana, citing Rav Natan bar Minyomi in the name of Rabbi Tanchum, expounds on the verse 'vehabor rek ein bo mayim', explaining that while there was no water, there were snakes and scorpions in the pit.

sub.text: Rav Kahana citing Rav Natan bar Minyomi in the name of Rabbi Tanchum
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana citing Rav Natan bar Minyomi in the name of Rabbi Tanchum
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana expounds on the verse 'vehabor rek ein bo mayim', explaining that while the pit had no water, it contained snakes and scorpions.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Elazar ben Chisma visiting Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Elazar ben Chisma visiting Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The Sages relate a story where Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Elazar ben Chisma visited Rabbi Yehoshua, who asked for a novel teaching from the study hall. They reported that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya had taught on the portion of Hakhel, explaining that children are brought to give reward to those who bring them, and he also expounded on the verses 'Atah he'emartah' and 'VaHashem he'emircha', teaching that Israel made God a unique entity in the world, and God will make them a unique entity.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the story of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Elazar ben Chisma visiting Rabbi Yehoshua, who asks for a novel teaching from the study hall.
Rabbi Yehoshua asks whose Shabbat it was and what was expounded in the portion of Hakhel.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's first teaching
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's first teaching
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya taught that children are brought to Hakhel to give reward to those who bring them, and Rabbi Yehoshua praises this as a precious pearl.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's second teaching
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's second teaching
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya further expounded on the verses 'Atah he'emartah' and 'VaHashem he'emircha'.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya concludes that Israel made God a unique entity in the world through the Shema, and God will make them a unique entity, citing the verse that follows.

items.text: Opening homily on the unity of Torah
items.text_en: Opening homily on the unity of Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara expounds on the verse comparing Torah to a goad and nails, explaining that Torah guides towards life, is not movable, and is fruitful. It then addresses the apparent contradictions among rabbinic rulings, concluding that all were given by one Shepherd, and encourages the listener to be open to all opinions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a verse praising Israel as a unique nation, then begins expounding the verse about the words of the sages being like goads and nails.
The Gemara rejects the analogy of a goad being movable, citing the word 'nails' to show Torah is fixed.
The Gemara rejects the analogy of a nail being deficient, citing the word 'planted' to show Torah is fruitful and multiplies.
The Gemara interprets 'masters of assemblies' as referring to groups of sages who issue contradictory rulings on purity, prohibition, and fitness.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by stating that all rulings were given by one Shepherd, one God, as the verse says 'God spoke all these words'.

Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah concludes the homily by exhorting the listener to make their ears like a funnel and acquire a heart to hear all opinions, declaring that no generation is orphaned when he is present.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Yossi ben Dormaskit and the ruling on Ammon and Moab
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yossi ben Dormaskit and the ruling on Ammon and Moab
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts an incident where Rabbi Yossi ben Dormaskit visited Rabbi Eliezer and reported a ruling that Ammon and Moab give the poor man's tithe in the seventh year. Rabbi Eliezer, distressed, caused Rabbi Yossi to lose his sight, then prayed for its restoration. He then revealed a tradition from Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai that this was a halakha from Sinai, explaining the reason.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah did not state the ruling about Ammon and Moab explicitly, and answers that it is because of an incident.
The baraita recounts the story of Rabbi Yossi ben Dormaskit visiting Rabbi Eliezer in Lod and being asked about the day's novelty in the study hall.
Rabbi Yossi reports that the sages voted and concluded that Ammon and Moab give the poor man's tithe in the seventh year.
Rabbi Eliezer, distressed, causes Rabbi Yossi to lose his sight and then weeps, citing a verse about God's secret being revealed to the God-fearing.
Rabbi Eliezer instructs Rabbi Yossi to tell the sages not to rely on their vote, as he has a tradition from Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai that this is a halakha from Sinai.

Rabbi Eliezer explains the reason: many cities conquered by those who left Egypt were not conquered by those who returned from Babylon, because the first sanctity was only for its time and not for the future, and they were left for the poor to rely on in the seventh year.
The tanna reports that after Rabbi Eliezer's mind was calmed, he prayed that Rabbi Yossi's eyes be restored, and they were.

items.text: Definition of a fool
items.text_en: Definition of a fool
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the definition of a fool, listing three behaviors: going out alone at night, sleeping in a cemetery, and tearing one's garment. A dispute arises between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan whether all three must be done simultaneously or even one suffices. The Gemara clarifies that if done in a crazy manner, even one qualifies, but if not, even all three do not.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines a fool by three behaviors: going out alone at night, sleeping in a cemetery, and tearing one's garment.

The Gemara questions the dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan, asking whether the behaviors must be done simultaneously or even one suffices, and clarifies that if done in a crazy manner even one qualifies, but if not even all three do not.
The Gemara resolves the dispute by explaining that each behavior could have a non-foolish motive, so only when all three are done together in a crazy manner does one qualify as a fool.

items.text: Rav Pappa's statement and the unresolved query about Rav Huna's retraction
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's statement and the unresolved query about Rav Huna's retraction
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says that if Rav Huna had heard the baraita defining a fool as one who loses everything given to him, he would have retracted his earlier statement. The Gemara then raises an unresolved question (teiku) about whether Rav Huna retracted only from the case of tearing garments or from all his statements.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that if Rav Huna had heard the baraita defining a fool as one who loses everything given to him, he would have retracted his earlier statement.
The Gemara raises an unresolved question (תיקו) whether Rav Huna retracted only from the case of tearing garments or from all his statements.

items.text: Baraita on the derivation of exemptions from 'zachur'
items.text_en: Baraita on the derivation of exemptions from 'zachur'
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that derives from the verses 'zachur', 'zechurcha', and 'kol zechurcha' the exemptions for women, tumtum and androgynos, and the inclusion of minors respectively.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that derives from the three forms of 'zachur' the exemptions for women, tumtum and androgynos, and the inclusion of minors.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer on the need for a verse to exempt women
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer on the need for a verse to exempt women
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a verse is needed to exempt women, since pilgrimage is a time-bound positive commandment from which women are generally exempt. It answers that a verse is necessary to counter a possible derivation from the 'hakhel' gathering where women are obligated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a verse is needed to exempt women from pilgrimage, since it is a time-bound positive commandment (מצות עשה שהזמן גרמא) from which women are generally exempt.

The Gemara answers that the verse is necessary to counter a possible גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the 'hakhel' gathering, where women are obligated, which might have led to obligating women in pilgrimage as well.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the exemption for tumtum and androgynos
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the exemption for tumtum and androgynos
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a verse is needed for androgynos to counter the notion that its male aspect obligates it. For tumtum, Abaye explains that the verse refers to a case where his testicles are external, making him a definite male but still excluded by the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that the verse 'זְכוּרְךָ' excludes a tumtum and androgynos, and acknowledges that for androgynos a verse is needed.
The Gemara questions why a verse is needed to exclude a tumtum, since he is merely a doubtful case and should be exempt without a verse.
Abaye answers that the verse refers to a tumtum whose testicles are external, making him a definite male who would otherwise be obligated, so a verse is needed to exclude him.

items.text: Reconciliation of the inclusion of minors with the Mishnah's exemption
items.text_en: Reconciliation of the inclusion of minors with the Mishnah's exemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the baraita includes minors via 'kol zechurcha', but a Mishnah exempts a minor. Abaye resolves that the baraita refers to a minor who has reached the age of chinuch (rabbinic obligation), and the verse is merely an asmakhta (support).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the baraita includes minors via 'כל זכורך', but a Mishnah explicitly exempts a minor.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a minor who has reached the age of חינוך (rabbinic obligation) and one who has not.
The Gemara objects that the obligation for a minor who has reached the age of חינוך is only rabbinic, not biblical.
The Gemara concedes that indeed the obligation is rabbinic, and the verse is merely an אסמכתא (supportive allusion).

items.text: Alternative interpretation of 'kol zechurcha' according to Acherim
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation of 'kol zechurcha' according to Acherim
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse 'kol zechurcha' actually comes for, and answers that it is for the view of Acherim, who exempt those who cannot ascend with all males, such as a copper smelter or tanner, due to their foul smell.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse 'כל זכורך' actually comes for, and answers that it is for the view of Acherim.
The Gemara cites the baraita of Acherim, who exempt those who cannot ascend with all males, such as a copper smelter or tanner, due to their foul smell.

items.text: Derivation of the exemption for slaves and the case of a half-slave half-free man
items.text_en: Derivation of the exemption for slaves and the case of a half-slave half-free man
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the exemption for slaves from the verse 'el penei ha'adon Hashem', excluding one who has another master. It questions why a verse is needed given the general rule that a slave's obligations mirror a woman's. Ravina answers that the verse is needed for a half-slave half-free man, and the Mishnah's phrasing supports this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: granted the exemption for women is derived as explained, but from where do we derive the exemption for slaves?
Rav Huna answers that the verse 'אֶל פְּנֵי הָאָדוֹן ה׳' (before the Lord God) excludes one who has another master, i.e., a slave.
The Gemara objects: why is a verse needed at all, since a slave's obligations mirror a woman's via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'לָהּ' 'לָהּ'?
Ravina resolves that the verse is needed for a half-slave half-free man, and the Mishnah's phrasing 'slaves who are not freed' supports this.

items.text: Exemption for the lame, blind, sick, and elderly from the word 'raglayim'
items.text_en: Exemption for the lame, blind, sick, and elderly from the word 'raglayim'
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from the word 'raglayim' (feet) an exemption for those with physical impairments preventing walking, including the lame, blind, sick, elderly, and one unable to walk. Rava adds that this also includes one who cannot walk on his feet.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites the verse 'רגלים' (feet) to exclude those with physical impairments (בעלי קבין) from the pilgrimage obligation.
The baraita offers an alternative interpretation: 'רגלים' excludes the lame, sick, blind, elderly, and one unable to walk on his feet.
The gemara asks: what additional case does the phrase 'one unable to walk on his feet' come to include?
Rava answers that the phrase comes to include one who cannot walk on his feet (even if not otherwise impaired).

items.text: Exemption of the uncircumcised and impure from re'iyah
items.text_en: Exemption of the uncircumcised and impure from re'iyah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that the uncircumcised and the impure are exempt from the pilgrimage. It explains the exemption for the impure from the verse 'and you shall come there' and 'and you shall bring there', linking coming and bringing. For the uncircumcised, it identifies the source as Rabbi Akiva's teaching that 'ish ish' includes the uncircumcised.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that the uncircumcised and the impure are exempt from the pilgrimage (רְאִיָּיה), and the Gemara explains the exemption for the impure from the verses 'וּבָאתָ שָּׁמָּה' (and you shall come there) and 'וַהֲבֵאתֶם שָׁמָּה' (and you shall bring there), linking the ability to come with the obligation to bring.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive the exemption for the uncircumcised?
The Gemara answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, who derives from the verse 'אִישׁ אִישׁ' (any man) to include the uncircumcised as equivalent to the impure.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan ben Dahavai's exemption for the one-eyed
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Dahavai's exemption for the one-eyed
items.desc_en: A baraita is taught: the impure is exempt from re'iyah, derived from the same verse. Rabbi Yochanan ben Dahavai says in the name of Rabbi Yehuda that a person blind in one eye is exempt, based on the play on words 'yir'eh' (he shall see) and 'yera'eh' (he shall be seen), requiring that just as one comes to see with two eyes, so too one must be seen with two eyes.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that an impure person is exempt from re'iyah (the pilgrimage appearance), derived from the verses 'ובאת שמה' (and you shall come there) and 'והבאתם שמה' (and you shall bring there), linking the ability to bring an offering with the ability to enter the Temple.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan ben Dahavai citing Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Dahavai citing Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Dahavai says in the name of Rabbi Yehuda that a person blind in one eye is exempt from re'iyah, based on the wordplay 'יִרְאֶה' (he shall see) and 'יֵרָאֶה' (he shall be seen), requiring that just as one comes to see with two eyes, so too one must be seen with two eyes.

items.text: Rav Huna's weeping over the verse 'ki tavo'u lera'ot panai'
items.text_en: Rav Huna's weeping over the verse 'ki tavo'u lera'ot panai'
items.desc_en: When Rav Huna reached the verse 'ki tavo'u lera'ot panai' (when you come to appear before Me), he wept, saying: A slave whose master expects to see him, yet he distances himself from him, as the verse continues 'mi bikesh zot miyedechem remos chatserai' (who required this from your hand, trampling My courts?).

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna weeps upon reaching the verse 'יִרְאֶה' 'יֵרָאֶה' (appear before Me), lamenting that a slave whose master expects to see him distances himself, as the verse continues 'מִי בִקֵּשׁ זֹאת מִיֶּדְכֶם רְמוֹס חֲצֵרָי' (who required this from your hand, trampling My courts?).

items.text: Rav Huna's weeping over the verse 'vezavachta shelamim'
items.text_en: Rav Huna's weeping over the verse 'vezavachta shelamim'
items.desc_en: When Rav Huna reached the verse 'vezavachta shelamim ve'achalta sham' (and you shall sacrifice peace offerings and eat there), he wept, questioning: A slave whose master expects to eat at his table, yet he distances himself? The verse 'lama li rov zichveichem' (why do I need your many sacrifices) shows God's rejection.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna weeps upon reaching the verse 'vezavachta shelamim ve'achalta sham' (and you shall sacrifice peace offerings and eat there), lamenting that a slave whose master expects to eat at his table would distance himself, as God says 'lama li rov zichveichem' (why do I need your many sacrifices).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's weeping over divine judgment and Samuel's fear
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's weeping over divine judgment and Samuel's fear
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar wept when reaching the verse about Joseph's brothers being unable to answer him, reasoning that if human rebuke is so powerful, divine rebuke is even more so. He also wept over Samuel's fear of judgment, as the witch of Endor saw 'elohim olim' (gods ascending), implying Samuel brought Moses with him, fearing judgment for any unfulfilled Torah law.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar weeps upon reaching the verse about Joseph's brothers being unable to answer him, reasoning that if human rebuke is so powerful, divine rebuke is even more so.
Rabbi Elazar weeps over Samuel's fear of judgment, as the witch of Endor saw 'אלוהים עולים' (gods ascending), implying Samuel brought Moses with him, fearing judgment for any unfulfilled Torah law.

items.text: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi's weeping over 'ulai' (perhaps)
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi's weeping over 'ulai' (perhaps)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami wept when reaching the verse 'yiten be'afar pihu ulai yesh tikvah' (let him put his mouth in the dust, perhaps there is hope), exclaiming: All this and still 'ulai' (perhaps)? Similarly, he wept over 'bakshu tzedek bakshu anavah ulai tisateru' (seek justice, seek humility, perhaps you will be hidden). Rabbi Asi wept over 'sin'u ra ve'ehavu tov... ulai yechonan' (hate evil, love good... perhaps He will be gracious), also exclaiming about the uncertainty.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami weeps upon reaching the verse 'יִתֵּן בֶּעָפָר פִּיהוּ אוּלַי יֵשׁ תִּקְוָה' (let him put his mouth in the dust, perhaps there is hope), exclaiming that after all this effort, the outcome is still only 'אוּלַי' (perhaps).
Rabbi Ami weeps again upon the verse 'בַּקְּשׁוּ צֶדֶק... אוּלַי תִּסָּתְרוּ' (seek justice... perhaps you will be hidden), similarly lamenting the uncertainty.
Rabbi Asi weeps upon the verse 'שִׂנְאוּ רָע... אוּלַי יֶחֱנַן' (hate evil... perhaps He will be gracious), also exclaiming about the uncertainty.

items.text: Rav Yosef's weeping over 'yesh nispeh belo mishpat' and the story of the Angel of Death
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's weeping over 'yesh nispeh belo mishpat' and the story of the Angel of Death
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef wept when reaching the verse 'veyesh nispeh belo mishpat' (there is one who is swept away without judgment), questioning if anyone dies before their time. He answers yes, citing the case of Rav Beivai bar Abaye, who was familiar with the Angel of Death. The Angel sent his agent to bring Miriam the hair-dresser, but the agent mistakenly brought Miriam the children's caretaker. When told of the error, the Angel said to keep her for the count, and asked how the agent managed to take her, as she was holding a weaver's tool and was...

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef weeps upon reaching the verse 'וְיֵשׁ נִסְפֶּה בְּלֹא מִשְׁפָּט' (there is one who is swept away without judgment) and asks rhetorically whether anyone dies before their appointed time.

Rav Yosef answers in the affirmative, citing the case of Rav Beivai bar Abaye who was familiar with the Angel of Death, who sent his agent to bring Miriam the hair-dresser but the agent mistakenly brought Miriam the children's caretaker.
When told of the error, the Angel of Death says to keep her for the count, and asks how the agent managed to take her, as she was holding a weaver's tool and was... (the story is cut off).

items.text: Story of Rav Bibi and the oven
items.text_en: Story of Rav Bibi and the oven
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi bar Abbaye questions a person who performed a seemingly miraculous act with an oven. The person justifies it with the verse 'And there is one who is destroyed without judgment,' but Rav Bibi counters with 'A generation goes and a generation comes.' The person explains he extends the lives of the righteous to fill the generation, then hands them over to the Angel of Death, and if a Torah scholar passes by, he adds to his years as a replacement.

sub.desc_en: The story opens with a person performing a seemingly miraculous act: he heats an oven, places it on his leg, and it cools without harming him.
Rav Bibi bar Abbaye asks the person whether he has permission to act in such a miraculous manner.
The person justifies his action by citing the verse 'And there is one who is destroyed without judgment,' implying he acts to prevent such unjust destruction.
Rav Bibi bar Abbaye objects by citing the verse 'A generation goes and a generation comes,' implying that death is natural and not to be interfered with.
The person explains that he extends the lives of the righteous to fill the generation, then hands them over to the Angel of Death (דומה).

sub.text: Rav Bibi bar Abbaye's follow-up question
sub.text_en: Rav Bibi bar Abbaye's follow-up question
sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi bar Abbaye asks what the person does about the years he has added to the righteous person's life.
The person explains that if a Torah scholar passes by, he adds to his years as a replacement for the years he added to the righteous person.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan weeps over divine enticement and lack of faith
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan weeps over divine enticement and lack of faith
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan weeps upon reaching the verse 'And you enticed me to swallow him for nothing,' questioning whether a servant whose master entices him has any remedy. He also weeps over 'Behold, He does not trust in His holy ones,' asking if He does not trust His holy ones, whom will He trust?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan weeps upon reaching the verse 'ותסיתני בו לבלעו חנם' (and you enticed me to swallow him for nothing), questioning whether a servant whose master entices him has any remedy.
Rabbi Yochanan weeps upon reaching the verse 'הן בקדושיו לא יאמין' (Behold, He does not trust in His holy ones), asking if He does not trust His holy ones, whom will He trust?

items.text: Story of the fig picker and the young student
items.text_en: Story of the fig picker and the young student
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan sees a man picking figs, leaving ripe ones for unripe ones, and learns that the unripe ones are better for travel. He applies the verse 'Behold, He does not trust in His holy ones.' The Gemara questions this with a story of a young student who died young, but explains that student was rebellious against his teachers.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan (רבי יוחנן) sees a man picking figs, leaving ripe ones for unripe ones, and learns that the unripe ones are better for travel.
Rabbi Yochanan (רבי יוחנן) applies the verse 'הן בקדושיו לא יאמין' (Behold, He does not trust in His holy ones) to this incident.
The Gemara questions this with a story of a young student who died young, implying that even righteous people die young.
The Gemara answers that the young student was rebellious against his teachers, so the verse does not apply to him.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan weeps over swift judgment
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan weeps over swift judgment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan weeps upon the verse 'And I will draw near to you for judgment, and I will be a swift witness,' questioning whether a servant whose master brings him to judgment and hastens to testify against him has any remedy.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan weeps upon encountering the verse about swift judgment, questioning whether a servant whose master hastens to testify against him has any remedy.

items.text: Sayings of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, Resh Lakish, and Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa
items.text_en: Sayings of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, Resh Lakish, and Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai laments that Scripture weighs light sins as heavily as severe ones. Resh Lakish says that one who perverts the judgment of a ger is as if perverting the judgment of Heaven. Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa says that one who does something and regrets it is immediately forgiven.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai laments that Scripture weighs light sins as heavily as severe ones.
Resh Lakish states that one who perverts the judgment of a ger (convert) is as if perverting the judgment of Heaven, citing a verse where the word is written defectively.
Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa states that one who does something and regrets it is immediately forgiven, citing a verse.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan weeps over hidden sins, and interpretations of 'every hidden thing'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan weeps over hidden sins, and interpretations of 'every hidden thing'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan weeps over the verse 'For God will bring every deed into judgment, concerning every hidden thing,' questioning whether a servant whose master weighs unintentional sins as intentional has any remedy. Rav and Shmuel interpret 'every hidden thing': Rav says it refers to killing a louse in front of a friend and being disgusted; Shmuel says it refers to spitting in front of a friend and being disgusted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan weeps upon reaching the verse about hidden sins, questioning whether a servant whose master weighs unintentional sins as intentional has any remedy.
The Gemara asks for the interpretation of the phrase 'על כל נעלם' (concerning every hidden thing).
Rav interprets 'every hidden thing' as referring to killing a louse in front of a friend and being disgusted by it.
Shmuel interprets 'every hidden thing' as referring to spitting in front of a friend and being disgusted by it.

items.text: Interpretations of 'whether good or evil'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'whether good or evil'
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yannai says 'whether good or evil' refers to one who gives charity to a poor person publicly, as Rabbi Yannai rebuked a man for doing so. The school of Rabbi Sheila says it refers to one who gives charity to a woman in secret, bringing suspicion. Rava says it refers to one who sends his wife uncut meat on Friday evenings, but the Gemara notes Rava himself did so, distinguishing his wife as knowledgeable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'whether good or evil' in the verse refers to.

The school of Rabbi Yannai says it refers to one who gives charity to a poor person publicly, as Rabbi Yannai rebuked a man for doing so, saying it would have been better not to give at all than to give and embarrass him.
The school of Rabbi Sheila says it refers to one who gives charity to a woman in secret, as it brings her under suspicion.
Rava says it refers to one who sends his wife uncut meat on Friday evenings, which could cause suspicion.
The Gemara objects that Rava himself used to send uncut meat to his wife on Friday evenings.
The Gemara resolves that the case of Rava's wife, the daughter of Rav Chisda, is different because he knew she was knowledgeable and would not suspect him.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan weeps over 'many evils and troubles', and interpretations
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan weeps over 'many evils and troubles', and interpretations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan weeps over the verse 'And many evils and troubles shall find him,' questioning whether a servant whose master brings evils and troubles upon him has any remedy. Rav interprets 'evils and troubles' as evils that become troubles for each other, like a hornet and a scorpion. Shmuel says it refers to one who provides money to a poor person at his time of distress, and Rava cites a folk saying about money for an entrance not being found, but for a hanging being found.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan weeps upon reaching the verse 'And many evils and troubles shall find him,' questioning whether a servant whose master brings evils and troubles upon him has any remedy.
The Gemara asks for the interpretation of the phrase 'evils and troubles'.
Rav interprets 'evils and troubles' as evils that become troubles for each other, like a hornet and a scorpion.
Shmuel interprets the phrase as referring to one who provides money to a poor person at his time of distress.
Rava cites a folk saying: money for an entrance is not found, but for a hanging it is found.

items.text: Interpretation of 'I will hide My face'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'I will hide My face'
items.desc_en: Rav Bardela bar Tavyomei says in the name of Rav: Whoever is not subject to the hiding of God's face is not from them; whoever is not subject to 'and it shall be for food' is not from them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'I will be angry with them on that day, and I will abandon them and hide My face from them.'

sub.text: Rav Bardela bar Tavyomei citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Bardela bar Tavyomei citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Bardela bar Tavyomei says in the name of Rav that anyone not included in the hiding of God's face is not from them, and anyone not included in 'and it shall be for food' is not from them.

items.text: Rava's encounter with divine hiddenness
items.text_en: Rava's encounter with divine hiddenness
items.desc_en: The rabbis tell Rava he is not subject to 'hiding of the face' or 'it shall be for eating.' Rava protests that he secretly sends gifts to King Shapur, but the rabbis fix their eyes on him, leading to his arrest. He cites Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel: wherever the sages fix their eyes, there is death or poverty.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis tell Rava that he is not subject to the punishments of 'hiding of the face' or 'it shall be for eating.'
Rava protests that the rabbis do not know how much he secretly sends to King Shapur's house.
Despite Rava's protest, the rabbis fix their eyes on him, and agents of King Shapur come and arrest him.
Rava cites a baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: wherever the sages fix their eyes, there is death or poverty.

items.text: Interpretations of 'I will surely hide My face'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'I will surely hide My face'
items.desc_en: Rava says that even when God hides His face, He speaks in dreams. Rav Yosef says His hand is still outstretched over us, citing 'in the shadow of My hand I have covered you.'

sub.desc_en: Rava interprets the verse 'I will surely hide My face' to mean that even in hiding, God speaks to Israel through dreams.
Rav Yosef offers an alternative interpretation: God's hand is still outstretched over Israel, citing the verse 'in the shadow of My hand I have covered you.'

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and the heretic at the Caesar's court
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and the heretic at the Caesar's court
items.desc_en: A heretic gestures to Rabbi Yehoshua that God has turned His face from Israel. Rabbi Yehoshua gestures back that God's hand is still outstretched. The Caesar asks what was communicated, and the heretic is killed for not understanding the gesture.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya stands at the Caesar's court; a heretic gestures that God has turned His face from Israel, and Rabbi Yehoshua gestures back that God's hand is still outstretched.
Caesar asks Rabbi Yehoshua what the heretic gestured to him, and Rabbi Yehoshua explains the exchange.
The court interrogates the heretic, who cannot explain his gesture, and they execute him for incompetence before the king.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's deathbed advice and alternative verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's deathbed advice and alternative verse
items.desc_en: On his deathbed, the rabbis ask Rabbi Yehoshua what will become of them regarding heretics. He says that when counsel is lost from Israel, the wisdom of the nations rots. An alternative source is offered from the verse about traveling.

sub.desc_en: On his deathbed, the rabbis ask Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya what will become of them regarding heretics.
Rabbi Yehoshua answers that when counsel is lost from Israel, the wisdom of the nations rots.
The Gemara offers an alternative verse from the story of traveling as a source for the same idea.

items.text: God reveals even idle conversation at death
items.text_en: God reveals even idle conversation at death
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila hears a child reciting a verse and infers that a servant whose master reveals his conversation has hope. Rav says even idle talk between a man and his wife is revealed at death. This is challenged by Rav Kahana's story of Rav's behavior, resolved by distinguishing when appeasement is needed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila hears a child reciting a verse and infers that a servant whose master reveals his conversation has hope.
Rav explains that even idle conversation between a man and his wife is revealed to him at the time of death.
Rav Kahana objects by recounting that he once heard Rav laughing and joking with his wife, yet Rav rebuked him for eavesdropping.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when appeasement of the wife is needed and when it is not.

items.text: God's weeping and the place of 'Mistarim'
items.text_en: God's weeping and the place of 'Mistarim'
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Inya says God has a place called 'Mistarim.' The verse 'because of pride' is interpreted as the pride of Israel given to nations, or the pride of heaven. The Gemara questions whether God weeps, resolving that He does not weep in the inner chambers, but the destruction of the Temple is exceptional.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Inya citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Inya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Inya cites the verse and states that God has a place called 'Mistarim'.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'because of pride' in the verse.
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak explains that 'because of pride' refers to the pride of Israel that was taken from them and given to the nations.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani offers an alternative interpretation: 'because of pride' refers to the pride of the kingdom of heaven.
The Gemara questions whether there is weeping before God, given that Rav Pappa stated there is no sadness before Him.
Rav Pappa objects by citing a verse that indicates joy and gladness are in God's place, implying no weeping.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the inner chambers (where there is no weeping) and the outer chambers (where weeping occurs).
The Gemara objects by citing a verse that calls for weeping and mourning, suggesting that even in the outer chambers there is weeping.
The Gemara resolves that the destruction of the Temple is exceptional, as even the angels wept over it.

items.text: Three tears for the exiles and nullification of Torah
items.text_en: Three tears for the exiles and nullification of Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains the three tears in the verse: one for the First Temple, one for the Second, and one for Israel's exile. Some say the third is for the nullification of Torah. The Gemara reconciles the latter with the verse's mention of 'the flock of the Lord.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets the three tears in the verse as referring to the First Temple, the Second Temple, and Israel's exile, with an alternative view that the third tear is for the nullification of Torah.
The Gemara questions how the alternative view that the third tear is for nullification of Torah fits the verse's mention of 'the flock of the Lord' being exiled.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that since Israel was exiled, there is no greater nullification of Torah than that.

items.text: Three types of people God weeps over daily
items.text_en: Three types of people God weeps over daily
items.desc_en: The rabbis taught that God weeps daily over three: one who can study Torah but does not, one who cannot study Torah but does, and a haughty leader over the community.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis taught that God weeps daily over three types of people: one who can study Torah but does not, one who cannot study Torah but does, and a haughty leader over the community.

items.text: Rabbi's reaction to the verse 'He cast from heaven to earth'
items.text_en: Rabbi's reaction to the verse 'He cast from heaven to earth'
items.desc_en: Rabbi was reading Lamentations and when he reached the verse 'He cast from heaven to earth,' the book fell from his hand. He remarked: from a high roof to a deep pit.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi was reading the book of Lamentations, and when he reached the verse 'He cast from heaven to earth,' the book fell from his hand, and he remarked: from a high roof to a deep pit.

items.text: Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya greet a blind sage
items.text_en: Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya greet a blind sage
items.desc_en: Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya visit a blind Torah scholar. Rabbi Chiyya tells Rabbi not to demean his position. The blind sage blesses them: you greeted a face that sees but is not seen, may you merit greeting a face that sees but is not seen. Rabbi asks where he learned this, and the sage cites Rabbi Yaakov, who learned from his teacher that seeing sages in death grants life, all the more so in life.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya travel and decide to greet a blind Torah scholar in a town.
The blind sage blesses them: you greeted a face that sees but is not seen, may you merit greeting a face that sees but is not seen.
Rabbi asks the blind sage from whom he learned this blessing.
The blind sage cites Rabbi Yaakov's teaching: seeing sages in death grants life, all the more so in life.

items.text: The value of even one day of Torah study
items.text_en: The value of even one day of Torah study
items.desc_en: Rav Idi's father was mocked for spending only one day in the study hall. Rabbi Yochanan taught that one who studies Torah even one day a year is credited as if studying the whole year, and similarly for punishment.

sub.desc_en: Introduces Rav Idi, father of Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi, who was mocked by the rabbis for spending only one day in the study hall, causing him distress.
Rabbi Yochanan asks Rav Idi not to punish the rabbis for their mockery.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's teaching in the study hall
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's teaching in the study hall
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches in the study hall that one who studies Torah even one day a year is credited as if studying the whole year, citing the verse 'וְאוֹתִי יוֹם יוֹם יִדְרֹשׁוּן'.
The Gemara extends the same principle to punishment: one who commits a transgression even one day a year is considered as if he transgressed the whole year, citing the verse about the spies.

items.text: Definition of a minor
items.text_en: Definition of a minor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines a minor as one who cannot ride on his father's shoulder. Rabbi Zeira challenges this.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines a minor (קטן) as one who cannot ride on his father's shoulder.
Rabbi Zeira challenges this definition, implying it is insufficient or problematic.

items.text: Gemara's question and Abaye's answer about the minor's obligation
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Abaye's answer about the minor's obligation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the author of the earlier statement that a minor is obligated from when his mother is obligated in simchah. Abaye answers that the mother brings him, and from that point onward, if he can hold his father's hand from Jerusalem to the Temple Mount, he is obligated; otherwise, he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who brings the minor to the Temple for the obligation of simchah (rejoicing).

Abaye answers that the mother brings the minor while she is obligated in simchah; thereafter, if the minor can hold his father's hand from Jerusalem to the Temple Mount, he is obligated, otherwise exempt.

items.text: Rabbi's objection from Hannah and Samuel, and the father's response
items.text_en: Rabbi's objection from Hannah and Samuel, and the father's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi (under Beit Hillel) objects from the case of Hannah and Samuel, where Samuel could ride on his father's shoulder, yet Hannah did not bring him until he was weaned. His father responds that Hannah herself was obligated in simchah, but she was overly indulgent and worried about the journey's hardship.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi objects to the previous ruling by citing the case of Hannah and Samuel, where Samuel could ride on his father's shoulder yet Hannah did not bring him until weaned.
The father of Rabbi responds that Hannah herself was obligated in simchah, but she was overly indulgent and worried about the journey's hardship for Samuel.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's query about a lame or blind minor
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's query about a lame or blind minor
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon asks: what is the law for a lame minor (according to Beit Shammai) or a blind minor (according to both)? The Gemara clarifies that the question is only relevant when the minor can stretch (if lame) or open his eyes (if blind), since if he cannot, even an adult is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon asks about the obligation of a lame minor according to Beit Shammai, or a blind minor according to both schools.
The Gemara clarifies that the question is only relevant when the lame minor can stretch or the blind minor can open his eyes, since otherwise even an adult is exempt.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on training a minor
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on training a minor
items.desc_en: Abaye rules: wherever an adult is obligated by Torah law, we train the minor rabbinically; wherever an adult is exempt by Torah law, the minor is also exempt rabbinically.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that a minor is trained rabbinically wherever an adult is obligated by Torah law, and exempt rabbinically wherever an adult is exempt by Torah law.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute: Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hillel on re'iyah and chagigah values
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute: Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hillel on re'iyah and chagigah values
items.desc_en: The baraita states: Beit Shammai say the re'iyah offering is two silver pieces and the chagigah is one ma'ah, because the re'iyah is entirely for the Most High, unlike chagigah, and because at Shavuot the Torah increased burnt-offerings over peace-offerings. Beit Hillel say the re'iyah is one ma'ah and the chagigah is two silver pieces, because chagigah existed before the Giving of the Torah, unlike re'iyah, and because the princes offered more peace-offerings than burnt-offerings.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Beit Shammai's ruling on the minimum values of the re'iyah and chagigah offerings.
The baraita elaborates Beit Shammai's reasoning: the re'iyah is entirely burnt for the Most High, unlike chagigah, and at Shavuot the Torah increased burnt-offerings over peace-offerings.
The baraita presents Beit Hillel's ruling and reasoning: chagigah existed before the Giving of the Torah, unlike re'iyah, and the princes offered more peace-offerings than burnt-offerings.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: Beit Hillel's reasoning against Beit Shammai, and vice versa
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Beit Hillel's reasoning against Beit Shammai, and vice versa
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Beit Hillel reject Beit Shammai's arguments: the re'iyah's advantage (entirely for the Most High) is countered by chagigah's advantage (two eatings), and the analogy to Shavuot is invalid because one cannot derive an individual's offering from a communal one. Similarly, Beit Shammai reject Beit Hillel's arguments: chagigah's advantage (existed before the Giving of the Torah) applies also to re'iyah, and the analogy to the princes is invalid because one cannot derive a permanent practice from a temporary one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Beit Hillel do not accept Beit Shammai's reasoning.

The Gemara explains Beit Hillel's rejection: chagigah's advantage of two eatings outweighs re'iyah's advantage, and the analogy to Shavuot is invalid because one cannot derive an individual's offering from a communal one.
The Gemara asks why Beit Shammai do not accept Beit Hillel's reasoning.

The Gemara explains Beit Shammai's rejection: re'iyah also existed before the Giving of the Torah, and the analogy to the princes is invalid because one cannot derive a permanent practice from a temporary one.

items.text: Further dispute: the wilderness offerings as proof
items.text_en: Further dispute: the wilderness offerings as proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why does Beit Hillel claim chagigah existed before the Giving of the Torah? They cite the verse 'they sacrificed peace-offerings' (Exodus 24:5). But re'iyah also existed, as 'they offered burnt-offerings' (ibid.). Beit Hillel hold that the burnt-offering in the wilderness was the daily tamid, not a re'iyah offering, while Beit Shammai hold it was a re'iyah offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Beit Hillel: why do you claim chagigah existed before the Giving of the Torah based on the verse 'they sacrificed peace-offerings' (Exodus 24:5), when re'iyah also existed, as the same verse says 'they offered burnt-offerings'?
Beit Hillel hold that the burnt-offering brought by Israel in the wilderness was the daily tamid, not a re'iyah offering.
Beit Shammai hold that the burnt-offering brought by Israel in the wilderness was a re'iyah offering.

items.text: Abaye's list of tannaim aligned with each view
items.text_en: Abaye's list of tannaim aligned with each view
items.desc_en: Abaye states: Beit Shammai, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Yishmael all hold that the wilderness burnt-offering was a re'iyah offering. Beit Hillel, Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili hold it was the daily tamid. The Gemara begins to cite a baraita with Rabbi Yishmael's opinion.

sub.desc_en: Abaye lists the tannaim aligned with each view: Beit Shammai, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Yishmael hold the wilderness burnt-offering was a re'iyah offering; Beit Hillel, Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili hold it was the daily tamid.
The Gemara begins to cite a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael states that general principles were stated at Sinai, supporting his alignment with Beit Shammai's view.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to the assumption that the wilderness burnt-offering was the tamid
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to the assumption that the wilderness burnt-offering was the tamid
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the view that the burnt-offering brought by Israel in the wilderness was the daily tamid, arguing that if it were the tamid, it would require flaying and cutting up, but initially it did not require these, creating a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that the burnt-offering brought by Israel in the wilderness was the daily tamid, arguing that if it were the tamid, it would require flaying and cutting up, but initially it did not require these, creating a contradiction.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Akiva on the wilderness burnt-offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Akiva on the wilderness burnt-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar holds that the laws of the tamid were given at Sinai but the offering itself was not brought. Rabbi Akiva argues that it was brought and never ceased, interpreting the verse about no sacrifices in the wilderness as referring to the tribe of Levi who did not worship the golden calf.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Elazar holds that the laws of the tamid were given at Sinai but the offering itself was not brought.
Rabbi Akiva argues that the tamid was brought and never ceased, interpreting the verse about no sacrifices in the wilderness as referring to the tribe of Levi who did not worship the golden calf.

items.text: Rabbi Yose HaGelili on the three pilgrimage mitzvot
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose HaGelili on the three pilgrimage mitzvot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose HaGelili enumerates three commandments given to Israel upon ascending for the festival: re'iyah (appearance-offering), chagigah (festival-offering), and simchah (rejoicing). He then distinguishes each: re'iyah is entirely for the Most High, chagigah applies before the giving of the Torah, and simchah applies to both men and women.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yose HaGelili opens by stating that Israel was commanded three mitzvot upon ascending for the festival: re'iyah (appearance-offering), chagigah (festival-offering), and simchah (rejoicing).
The baraita begins distinguishing re'iyah from the other two: re'iyah is entirely for the Most High (a burnt-offering), unlike chagigah and simchah.
The baraita continues distinguishing chagigah: it applies before the giving of the Torah (i.e., the Sinaitic revelation), unlike re'iyah and simchah.
The baraita concludes distinguishing simchah: it applies to both men and women, unlike re'iyah and chagigah.

items.text: Gemara's defense of Rabbi Yishmael's position and citation of Rabbi Yose HaGelili
items.text_en: Gemara's defense of Rabbi Yishmael's position and citation of Rabbi Yose HaGelili
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yishmael is placed with Beit Shammai, and argues that if the wilderness burnt-offering were the tamid, the contradiction about flaying and cutting up would arise. It then cites a baraita where Rabbi Yose HaGelili explicitly states that the wilderness burnt-offering did not require flaying and cutting up, as these only apply from the Tent of Meeting onward, thus supporting Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yishmael is placed with Beit Shammai, arguing that if the wilderness burnt-offering were the tamid, the contradiction about flaying and cutting up would arise.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yose HaGelili explicitly holds the wilderness burnt-offering was the tamid, yet he still requires flaying and cutting up later.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yose HaGelili explicitly states that the wilderness burnt-offering did not require flaying and cutting up, as these only apply from the Tent of Meeting onward, thus supporting Rabbi Yishmael.

items.text: Rav Chisda's query about the animals in the wilderness offering
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's query about the animals in the wilderness offering
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks whether the verse 'They sent the young men of Israel and they offered burnt-offerings' refers to lambs, and 'they sacrificed peace-offerings' to oxen, or whether both were oxen. Mar Zutra says the difference is for the division of verses, while Rav Acha bar Rava says it matters for one who vows to bring an offering like that of the wilderness. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks whether the verse 'וַיִּשְׁלַח אֶת נַעֲרֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וַיַּעֲלוּ עוֹלוֹת' refers to lambs and 'וַיִּזְבְּחוּ זְבָחִים שְׁלָמִים לַה׳' to oxen, or whether both were oxen.
Mar Zutra explains that the practical difference is for the division of verses (פיסוק טעמים).
Rav Acha bar Rava says the difference matters for one who vows to bring an offering like that of the wilderness, and the question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Introduction to the Mishnah on things without a fixed measure
items.text_en: Introduction to the Mishnah on things without a fixed measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite the Mishnah that lists things that have no fixed measure, setting up the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that lists things without a fixed measure.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and dispute over the measure of re'iyah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and dispute over the measure of re'iyah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists re'iyah among things without a fixed measure. Rabbi Yochanan initially thought it has no upper limit but has a lower limit, until Rabbi Oshaya taught it has no limit at all. The Sages, however, set a fixed minimum: one ma'ah for re'iyah and two for chagigah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items without a fixed measure, including re'iyah (appearance offering).
Rabbi Yochanan initially thought re'iyah has no upper limit but has a lower limit.
Rabbi Oshaya taught that re'iyah has no limit at all, neither upper nor lower.
The Sages set a fixed minimum: one ma'ah for re'iyah and two for chagigah.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the definition of re'iyah
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the definition of re'iyah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan defines re'iyah as appearance in the Temple courtyard, while Reish Lakish defines it as appearance with a sacrifice. They agree that on the main festival day it requires a sacrifice, but disagree about other days: Rabbi Yochanan holds that if one comes without a sacrifice, he still fulfills the obligation, while Reish Lakish requires a sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the meaning of 're'iyah' (appearance) in the context of the pilgrimage obligation?
Rabbi Yochanan defines re'iyah as appearance in the Temple courtyard (עזרה) without requiring a sacrifice.
Reish Lakish defines re'iyah as appearance with a sacrifice (קרבן).

The Gemara clarifies that both agree on the main festival day (עיקר הרגל) that appearance requires a sacrifice; their dispute is about other days of the festival when one comes without bringing a sacrifice.

The Gemara explains: Rabbi Yochanan holds that appearance in the courtyard suffices and one need not bring a sacrifice on other days, while Reish Lakish holds that appearance requires a sacrifice whenever one comes.

items.text: Reish Lakish's objections and Rabbi Yochanan's responses
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's objections and Rabbi Yochanan's responses
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish brings three proofs that re'iyah requires a sacrifice: the verse 'Do not appear before Me empty-handed', a baraita comparing re'iyah to chagigah, and Rabbi Yose's statement that one must not appear empty-handed. Rabbi Yochanan deflects each by saying the verse applies only to the main festival day.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish objects to Rabbi Yochanan by citing the verse 'וְלֹא יֵרָאוּ פָנַי רֵיקָם' (Do not appear before Me empty-handed), implying that an offering is required whenever one appears.
Rabbi Yochanan responds that the verse applies only to the main day of the festival, not to the rest of the festival days.
Reish Lakish brings a baraita that interprets 'וְלֹא יֵרָאוּ פָנַי רֵיקָם' as requiring animal offerings, using a logical derivation from the chagigah offering.
Reish Lakish continues the baraita, specifying that the animal offerings are burnt-offerings (עוֹלוֹת), derived from the principle that what is fitting for God is a burnt-offering.
Reish Lakish adds a supporting argument: one's own table should not be full while the Master's table (the altar) is empty, implying a burnt-offering is required.
Rabbi Yochanan again responds that this obligation applies only to the main day of the festival.
Reish Lakish objects with a statement from Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Yehuda that one may not appear empty-handed, citing the same verse.
Rabbi Yochanan responds once more that the requirement applies only to the main day of the festival.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's counter-objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's counter-objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects to Reish Lakish using the verse 'yera'eh yir'eh' to argue that just as God appears freely, so too the Israelites appear freely. The Gemara then clarifies the actual dispute: when one comes without a sacrifice, all agree he may enter and leave; the dispute is when he brings a sacrifice, whether it has a fixed measure.

sub.desc_en: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) objects to ריש לקיש (Reish Lakish) by citing the verse 'יֵרָאֶה יִרְאֶה' (shall appear / will see), arguing that just as God appears for free, so too the Israelites may appear without an offering.
The Gemara resolves the dispute: when one comes without a sacrifice, all agree he may enter and leave; the dispute is only when he brings a sacrifice.

The Gemara explains the positions: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) holds that the appearance itself has no measure but the sacrifice does, while ריש לקיש (Reish Lakish) holds that even the sacrifice has no measure.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Levi about frequenting the Temple
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Levi about frequenting the Temple
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse 'Make your foot rare from your neighbor's house' to argue against bringing sacrifices too often. Rabbi Levi resolves the apparent contradiction between this verse and 'I will come into Your house with burnt offerings' by distinguishing between sin offerings and guilt offerings (which one should avoid) and burnt offerings and peace offerings (which are encouraged). A baraita supports this distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the verse 'Make your foot rare from your neighbor's house' and immediately answers that it refers to sin offerings and guilt offerings.
Rabbi Levi resolves the apparent contradiction between the two verses by distinguishing between sin/guilt offerings (avoid) and burnt/peace offerings (encourage).
A baraita explicitly supports Rabbi Levi's distinction, stating that the verse 'Make your foot rare' speaks only of sin offerings and guilt offerings.

items.text: Rav Yosef's inference about appearing in halves
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's inference about appearing in halves
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef infers from the Mishnah's statement that one may not appear in halves that a man with ten sons should not send five today and five tomorrow, but rather all must appear together.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef infers from the Mishnah's rule that one may not appear in halves that a man with ten sons should not bring five today and five tomorrow, but all must appear together.

items.text: Abaye's question and the source for the exemption of certain workers
items.text_en: Abaye's question and the source for the exemption of certain workers
items.desc_en: Abaye questions the necessity of the verse cited earlier, arguing that the exemption of certain workers is obvious. He then explains that the verse comes to teach the ruling of Aḥerim, who exempt a handful of workers from the pilgrimage obligation because they cannot ascend with all males.

sub.desc_en: Abaye questions the necessity of the verse, arguing that the exemption of certain workers is obvious and asking which workers are considered negligent and which diligent.
Abaye explains that the verse comes to teach the ruling of Aḥerim, who exempt a handful of workers from the pilgrimage obligation because they cannot ascend with all males.

items.text: Mishnah: Sources for offerings on the Festival and obligations of Israelites and priests
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sources for offerings on the Festival and obligations of Israelites and priests
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that burnt offerings brought on the intermediate days of a Festival come from non-sacred animals, while peace offerings come from tithed animals. It then discusses the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the first day of Passover, and lists which offerings fulfill the obligation for Israelites and priests.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that burnt offerings on the intermediate days come from non-sacred animals, while peace offerings come from tithed animals, and then records the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the first day of Passover.

The Mishnah lists which offerings fulfill the obligation for Israelites (vows, freewill offerings, and animal tithe) and for priests (sin offerings, guilt offerings, firstborn, and breast and thigh), excluding birds and meal offerings.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why are burnt offerings on the Festival from non-sacred animals?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why are burnt offerings on the Festival from non-sacred animals?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that burnt offerings on the Festival come from non-sacred animals, but on Yom Tov they would come from tithed animals. This is problematic because a burnt offering is an obligatory offering, which must come only from non-sacred animals. The Gemara then suggests that the Mishnah might follow Beit Shammai, who prohibit bringing burnt offerings on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah implies that burnt offerings on the Festival come from non-sacred animals, but on Yom Tov they would come from tithed animals, since an obligatory offering must come only from non-sacred animals.

The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah might follow Beit Shammai, who prohibit bringing burnt offerings on Yom Tov, thus the distinction between Festival and Yom Tov is about permissibility, not source.

items.text: Supporting baraita: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on bringing offerings on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Supporting baraita: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on bringing offerings on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Beit Shammai say one may bring peace offerings but not burnt offerings on Yom Tov, while Beit Hillel permit both. This supports the possibility that the Mishnah follows Beit Shammai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Beit Shammai permit bringing peace offerings but not burnt offerings on Yom Tov, while Beit Hillel permit both, supporting the possibility that the Mishnah follows Beit Shammai.

items.text: Resolution: The Mishnah is missing a clause and is reinterpreted
items.text_en: Resolution: The Mishnah is missing a clause and is reinterpreted
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by asserting that the Mishnah is incomplete and should be read as follows: Votive and freewill burnt offerings come on the intermediate days but not on Yom Tov; the obligatory burnt offering of appearance comes even on Yom Tov and only from non-sacred animals; peace offerings of rejoicing come even from tithed animals; and the dispute about the first day of Passover remains. A baraita supports this interpretation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by asserting that the Mishnah is incomplete and provides the corrected version: votive and freewill burnt offerings come on the intermediate days but not on Yom Tov; the obligatory burnt offering of appearance comes even on Yom Tov and only from non-sacred animals; peace offerings of rejoicing come even from tithed animals; and the dispute about the first day of Passover remains.
A baraita is cited that supports the Gemara's reinterpretation of the Mishnah, repeating the same corrected version.

items.text: Rav Ashi's clarification: Only the Festival of the 15th, not the 14th
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's clarification: Only the Festival of the 15th, not the 14th
