items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains why the Mishnah specifies the first day of Passover: it teaches that the obligation applies to the Festival of the 15th (the first day of Passover) but not to the 14th (the day before Passover).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifically mentions the Festival peace-offering of the first day of Passover.
Rav Ashi answers that the specification teaches that the obligation applies only to the Festival of the 15th (the first day of Passover), not to the 14th (the day before Passover).

items.text: Conclusion that chagigah on the 14th is not Torah-mandated
items.text_en: Conclusion that chagigah on the 14th is not Torah-mandated
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes from the previous discussion that Beit Hillel's view implies the chagigah on the 14th of Nisan is not a Torah obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Beit Hillel's position implies the chagigah on the 14th of Nisan is not a Torah obligation.

items.text: Dispute about tofel: attaching animals vs. money
items.text_en: Dispute about tofel: attaching animals vs. money
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Beit Hillel allows bringing the chagigah from ma'aser, since it is a chovah (obligation) which normally requires unconsecrated animals. Ulla answers that it is through tofel (attaching). Then Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan dispute whether one can attach an animal to another animal or money to money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Beit Hillel permits bringing the chagigah from ma'aser, since it is a חובה (obligation) that normally requires unconsecrated animals.
Ulla answers that the chagigah is brought through טופל (attaching it to the peace offering).
Chizkiyah states that one may attach an animal to another animal, but not money to money.
Rabbi Yochanan states that one may attach money to money, but not an animal to another animal.

items.text: Two baraitot supporting both views
items.text_en: Two baraitot supporting both views
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one supports Rabbi Yochanan's view that one may attach money to money, and another supports Chizkiyah's view that one may attach an animal to an animal. The baraitot also record the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel about when the chagigah must come from unconsecrated animals.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces two baraitot: one supporting Chizkiyah's view and one supporting Rabbi Yochanan's view, and cites the first baraita that supports Rabbi Yochanan, deriving from the verse 'מִסַּת' that one brings one's obligation from unconsecrated animals and may mix funds.

The gemara cites the second baraita that supports Chizkiyah, which records the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel: Beit Shammai says the first day must be from unconsecrated animals and thereafter from maaser (tithe), while Beit Hillel says the first meal must be from unconsecrated animals and thereafter from maaser.

items.text: Why ma'aser behemah is not used on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Why ma'aser behemah is not used on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one cannot fulfill one's obligation with ma'aser behemah on the rest of Pesach (Yom Tov). Rav Ashi answers that one might come to tithe on Yom Tov, which is forbidden due to the red mark (sekarta).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one cannot fulfill one's obligation with מעשר בהמה (animal tithe) on Yom Tov, given that it is permitted on the rest of Pesach.
Rav Ashi answers that one might come to tithe (לעשורי) on Yom Tov, which is forbidden because of the red mark (סקרתא) used for tithing.

items.text: Proof that 'masat' means unconsecrated
items.text_en: Proof that 'masat' means unconsecrated
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves that the word 'masat' in the verse refers to unconsecrated property, citing the verse about King Achashverosh imposing a tax (mas) on the land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the word 'מסת' (masat) refers to unconsecrated property (חולין).
The Gemara answers by citing the verse where King Achashverosh imposed a tax (מס) on the land, showing that 'מס' means a levy from unconsecrated property.

items.text: What Israelites and Kohanim use for simchah
items.text_en: What Israelites and Kohanim use for simchah
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that Israelites fulfill their obligation of rejoicing with nedarim, nedavot, and ma'aser behemah, while Kohanim use chatat, asham, bechor, and the breast and thigh. The verse excludes birds and meal-offerings.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that Israelites fulfill their obligation of rejoicing with nedarim, nedavot, and ma'aser behemah.
The baraita specifies that Kohanim fulfill their obligation with chatat, asham, bechor, and the breast and thigh.
The baraita excludes birds and meal-offerings by citing the verse 'ושמחת בחגך' (and you shall rejoice on your festival).

items.text: Exclusion from chagigah and scriptural derivation
items.text_en: Exclusion from chagigah and scriptural derivation
items.desc_en: The baraita states that those from whom the chagigah cannot be brought are excluded. Rav Ashi derives this from the word 'vesamachta', excluding those incapable of joy. The verse 'bechagecha' is then used for Rabbi Daniel bar Katina's teaching that one may not marry during the festival.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that those from whom the chagigah can be brought are included, excluding those from whom it cannot be brought.
Rav Ashi derives the exclusion from the word 'וְשָׂמַחְתָּ' (and you shall rejoice), excluding those incapable of joy.

sub.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Daniel bar Katina's teaching
sub.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Daniel bar Katina's teaching
sub.desc_en: The gemara asks what Rav Ashi does with the verse 'בְּחַגֶּךָ' (on your festival), and cites Rabbi Daniel bar Katina's teaching that one may not marry during the festival, derived from 'וְשָׂמַחְתָּ בְּחַגֶּךָ' (and you shall rejoice on your festival) and not with your wife.

items.text: Mishnah: Offerings according to means
items.text_en: Mishnah: Offerings according to means
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one with many eaters but few assets brings many shelamim and few olot; with many assets but few eaters, many olot and few shelamim. If both are few, the minimum applies; if both are many, one gives according to one's ability.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for one with many eaters but few assets: he brings many shelamim and few olot.
The Mishnah states the opposite case: many assets but few eaters brings many olot and few shelamim.
The Mishnah states that when both eaters and assets are few, the minimum of a ma'ah and two silver coins applies.
The Mishnah concludes that when both are many, one gives according to one's ability, as the verse states.

items.text: Gemara: How does a poor person bring many shelamim?
items.text_en: Gemara: How does a poor person bring many shelamim?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how one with few assets can bring many shelamim. Rav Chisda answers that he can attach and bring a large ox. Rav Sheishes objects, citing that they said one may attach an animal to an animal, implying a limit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how a person with few assets can bring many shelamim, since he lacks the means.
Rav Chisda answers that he can attach (טוֹפֵל) and bring a large ox, thereby fulfilling the requirement with one expensive animal.
Rav Sheishes objects, citing that the established rule permits attaching an animal to an animal, implying a limit that does not allow attaching money to an animal.

items.text: Clarification of Rav Sheishes' objection and the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Clarification of Rav Sheishes' objection and the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Sheishes meant they said one may attach an animal to an animal, but not money to money. It then questions whose opinion this follows, noting it aligns with neither Chizkiyah nor Rabbi Yochanan. The Mishnah's phrase 'first eating from chullin' is reinterpreted as the value of the first eating from chullin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion Rav Sheshet's statement follows, noting it aligns with neither חִזְקִיָּה (Chizkiyah) nor רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן (Rabbi Yochanan).

The Gemara objects that if one claims the dispute is only among אמוראים (Amora'im) but not in the ברייתות (baraitot), the baraita explicitly teaches 'first eating from חולין (non-sacred property)', contradicting that assumption.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by reinterpreting 'first eating' as the monetary value of the first eating from חולין (non-sacred property), not the entire animal.

items.text: Dispute between Ulla and Rabbi Yochanan about offering on the second festival day
items.text_en: Dispute between Ulla and Rabbi Yochanan about offering on the second festival day
items.desc_en: Ulla citing Reish Lakish says if one set aside ten animals for his chagigah and offered five on the first day, he may offer the remaining five on the second day. Rabbi Yochanan says once he stopped, he may not offer them. Rabbi Abba resolves that they disagree only in an unspecified case, but in a specified case they agree. The Gemara clarifies the unspecified case and concludes that the resolution is correct.

sub.desc_en: Ulla (עולא) reports in the name of ריש לקיש (Reish Lakish) that if one set aside ten animals for his חגיגה (Festival peace-offering) and offered five on the first יום טוב (festival day), he may offer the remaining five on the second יום טוב.
רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) states the opposing view: once he stopped after the first day, he may no longer sacrifice the remaining animals.
רבי אבא (Rabbi Abba) resolves the dispute: they do not disagree; one case is סתם (unspecified) and the other is מפרש (explicitly specified).
The גמרא (Gemara) asks: what are the circumstances of the unspecified case? It first suggests that there was no time left in the day to sacrifice.
The גמרא rejects the first suggestion and proposes instead that he lacked eaters, so he did not sacrifice them.

The גמרא (Gemara) concludes: the case is where there is time and eaters, yet he did not sacrifice them on the first day, so he intentionally left them over, and therefore may not sacrifice them later.

The גמרא (Gemara) notes that it is reasonable, because when רבין (Ravin) came he said that רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) ruled that one may sacrifice the remaining five on the second day, which contradicts the earlier statement of רבי יוחנן.
The גמרא (Gemara) concludes: must we not learn from this that here it is an unspecified case and there it is a specified case? Indeed, conclude so.

items.text: Supporting statement from Rav Shemen bar Abba
items.text_en: Supporting statement from Rav Shemen bar Abba
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a supporting tradition: Rav Shemen bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, confirming the earlier resolution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a supporting tradition: Rav Shemen bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, confirming the earlier resolution.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's 'gamur'
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's 'gamur'
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's distinction between one who 'finished' (גמר) and one who did not. It explains that 'gamur' refers to finishing the day, not the offerings, and that one who finished the day must bring a make-up offering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the rule applies only when one did not finish, but if he finished, he may go back and sacrifice.
The Gemara asks what 'gamur' means, suggesting it cannot mean finishing the offerings because then there would be nothing to sacrifice.
The Gemara explains that 'gamur' refers to finishing the day, not the offerings, and one who finished the day may return and sacrifice.

items.text: Mishnah: Make-up for missing the festival and interpretations of 'me'uvat'
items.text_en: Mishnah: Make-up for missing the festival and interpretations of 'me'uvat'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who did not celebrate on the first day of Sukkot may make up during the rest of the festival and the last day. After the festival, there is no further obligation. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya and Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai offer interpretations of the verse 'me'uvat lo yuchal litkon'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who did not celebrate on the first day of Sukkot may make up during the rest of the festival and the last day.
The Mishnah rules that after the festival passes, there is no further obligation, citing the verse 'me'uvat lo yuchal litkon'.
Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya interprets 'me'uvat' as one who engaged in intercourse with a forbidden woman and fathered a mamzer, which cannot be rectified, unlike theft which can be returned.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai interprets 'me'uvat' as a Torah scholar who leaves Torah study, someone initially straight who became crooked.

items.text: Gemara: Source for make-up from 'Atzeret'
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for make-up from 'Atzeret'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael derives the concept of make-up (תשלומין) for Sukkot from a verbal analogy between 'Atzeret' mentioned on the seventh day of Passover and 'Atzeret' on the eighth day of Sukkot. The Gemara explains that the term 'Atzeret' is superfluous and thus available for this derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the halacha of make-up (תשלומין) for Sukkot, and Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael begins to answer.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives the concept of make-up (תשלומין) for Sukkot from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'Atzeret' mentioned on the seventh day of Passover and 'Atzeret' on the eighth day of Sukkot.
The Gemara objects that the verbal analogy requires the term 'Atzeret' to be superfluous (מופנה), otherwise one could refute the analogy by noting differences between the two festivals.
The Gemara resolves that the term 'Atzeret' is indeed superfluous (מופנה) because the prohibition of work is already stated explicitly, so the extra word is available for the verbal analogy.

items.text: Alternative source from 'Vechagotem oto'
items.text_en: Alternative source from 'Vechagotem oto'
items.desc_en: A Tanna derives the make-up obligation from the verse 'Vechagotem oto chag la'Hashem shiv'at yamim', interpreting 'oto' to limit the celebration to the festival period, and 'shiv'ah' to allow make-up throughout the seven days. Another verse 'Bachodesh hashevi'i tachogu oto' extends the make-up to the entire month but is limited by 'oto'.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna derives the make-up obligation from the verse 'וְחַגּוֹתֶם אוֹתוֹ חַג לַה׳ שִׁבְעַת יָמִים', interpreting 'אוֹתוֹ' to limit the celebration to the festival period, and 'שִׁבְעָה' to allow make-up throughout the seven days.
Another verse 'בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִי תָּחֹגּוּ אוֹתוֹ' extends the make-up to the entire month but is limited by 'אוֹתוֹ' to the festival period.

items.text: Debate: Make-up for the first day or interchangeable
items.text_en: Debate: Make-up for the first day or interchangeable
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Oshaya debate whether the make-up days are for the first day (תשלומין לראשון) or interchangeable (תשלומין זה לזה). Rabbi Zeira explains the practical difference: a person who was lame on the first day but healed on the second. According to Rabbi Yochanan, since he was unfit on the first day, he cannot make up; according to Rabbi Oshaya, he can.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the nature of the make-up days (תשלומין) is.
Rabbi Yochanan states that the make-up days are תשלומין לראשון (make-up for the first day).
Rabbi Oshaya states that the make-up days are תשלומין זה לזה (interchangeable make-up days).
The Gemara asks what the practical difference is between the two positions.
Rabbi Zeira explains the difference: a person lame on the first day but healed on the second — according to Rabbi Yochanan he cannot bring an offering, but according to Rabbi Oshaya he can.

items.text: Challenge from impurity at night and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from impurity at night and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's position from a case of impurity: Hezekiah says one who becomes impure during the day brings a make-up, but at night does not; Rabbi Yochanan says even at night he brings. Rabbi Yirmeya resolves that impurity is different because it has a make-up in the second Passover.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's position by asking whether he really holds that view.
Hezekiah states that one who becomes impure during the day brings a make-up offering, but at night does not.
Rabbi Yochanan counters that even at night one brings the make-up offering.
Rabbi Yirmeya resolves the contradiction by distinguishing impurity, which has a make-up opportunity in the second Passover.

items.text: Rav Papa's objection (incomplete)
items.text_en: Rav Papa's objection (incomplete)
items.desc_en: Rav Papa objects to the resolution, but the text is cut off. The argument is incomplete in this segment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa objects to the previous resolution, noting that it works only for the one who says Pesach (offers a second chance), but the text is cut off.

items.text: Question on the second day as a completion
items.text_en: Question on the second day as a completion
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the view that the second day is a completion of the first, asking what one who holds the second day is an independent festival would say.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the view that the second day is a completion of the first, asking what one who holds the second day is an independent festival would say.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's view on night and missing time
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's view on night and missing time
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that Rabbi Yochanan holds that night is not considered a missing time. The Gemara challenges this from a baraita about seeing discharges, and resolves that Rabbi Yochanan was speaking according to the one who says night is missing time, and the case of two by day and one at night was necessary to teach.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that Rabbi Yochanan holds that night is not considered a missing time (מחוסר זמן).
The Gemara challenges Rav Pappa's explanation, questioning whether Rabbi Yochanan actually holds this view.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling about seeing discharges: two by day and one at night brings an offering, but two at night and one by day does not, which seems to contradict the idea that night is not a missing time.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan was speaking according to the one who says night is a missing time, and the case of two by day and one at night was necessary to teach.
The Gemara adds that one might have thought like the strong objection of Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi, but the ruling teaches us like Rav Yosef.

items.text: Mishnah: One who missed the festival
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who missed the festival
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who passed the festival without celebrating is not liable for its replacement, and applies the verse 'Me'uvat lo yuchal litkon vechesron lo yuchal lehimanot'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who missed the festival is not liable for its replacement, citing the verse 'Me'uvat lo yuchal litkon vechesron lo yuchal lehimanot'.

items.text: Bar Hei Hei's question and the Tosefta's interpretation
items.text_en: Bar Hei Hei's question and the Tosefta's interpretation
items.desc_en: Bar Hei Hei questions the word 'lehimanot' and interprets it as referring to one whose friends were counted for a mitzvah but he was not. A Tosefta supports this, applying the verse to one who missed Shema or prayer, or who was not counted with his friends for a mitzvah.

sub.text: Bar Hei Hei's question to Hillel
sub.text_en: Bar Hei Hei's question to Hillel
sub.desc_en: Bar Hei Hei asks Hillel why the verse uses 'להימנות' (to be numbered) instead of 'להמלאות' (to be filled).
Hillel explains that the verse refers to one whose friends were counted for a mitzvah but he was not included.
A baraita supports Hillel's interpretation, applying 'מעוות לא יוכל לתקון' to one who missed Shema or prayer, and 'וחסרון לא יוכל להמנות' to one not counted with his friends for a mitzvah.

items.text: Bar Hei Hei's second question and the donkey market parable
items.text_en: Bar Hei Hei's second question and the donkey market parable
items.desc_en: Bar Hei Hei asks about the distinction between 'oved Elohim' and 'asher lo avado'. Hillel explains that both are completely righteous, but one who reviews his chapter 101 times is not comparable to one who reviews it 100 times, illustrated by the donkey market parable.

sub.desc_en: Bar Hei Hei asks Hillel about the redundancy in the verse from Malachi, noting that 'צדיק (righteous)' and 'עובד אלוהים (servant of God)' seem synonymous, as do 'רשע (wicked)' and 'אשר לא עבדו (one who does not serve Him)'.

Hillel explains that both 'עובד אלוהים (servant of God)' and 'אשר לא עבדו (one who does not serve Him)' refer to completely righteous people, but the distinction lies in the number of reviews: one who reviews his chapter 101 times is not comparable to one who reviews it 100 times.
Bar Hei Hei objects that it seems excessive to call someone 'אשר לא עבדו (one who does not serve Him)' merely for missing one review.

Hillel affirms his position and illustrates with a parable from the donkey market: traveling ten parasangs costs one dinar, but eleven parasangs costs two dinars, showing that a small extra effort yields a disproportionate difference.

items.text: Elijah's teaching on poverty and the folk saying
items.text_en: Elijah's teaching on poverty and the folk saying
items.desc_en: Elijah taught that God sought all good traits to give to Israel but found only poverty. Samuel or Rav Yosef cites a folk saying that poverty is becoming to Jews like a red bridle on a white horse.

sub.text: Elijah to Bar Hei Hei / Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Elijah to Bar Hei Hei / Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Elijah teaches that God sought all good traits for Israel but found only poverty.

sub.text: Samuel / Rav Yosef citing a folk saying
sub.text_en: Samuel / Rav Yosef citing a folk saying
sub.desc_en: Samuel or Rav Yosef cites a folk saying that poverty is becoming to Jews like a red bridle on a white horse.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai on 'Me'uvat'
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai on 'Me'uvat'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya applies the verse to one who commits adultery and begets a mamzer, but the Gemara questions if it applies only when a child is born. A baraita explains that one who commits adultery with a married woman cannot rectify it. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish discuss the Torah scholar who abandons Torah. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a single woman and a married woman.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya states that the verse 'me'uvat lo yuchal litkon' refers to one who commits adultery with a forbidden relative and begets a mamzer.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's statement implies that the verse applies only when a child is born, but not when no child is born.

A baraita is cited where Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya explains that a thief can rectify his sin by returning the stolen item, but one who commits adultery with a married woman cannot rectify it because he has rendered her forbidden to her husband.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai applies the verse to a Torah scholar who abandons Torah study, comparing him to a lamb that is inspected.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish adds that a Torah scholar who abandons Torah is compared to a bird that leaves its nest, and cites a verse about distancing from God.

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's statements by distinguishing between a single woman (where no child is needed for the sin to be irreparable) and a married woman (where the sin is irreparable regardless of offspring).

items.text: Resolution of a contradiction about a married woman who drinks wine
items.text_en: Resolution of a contradiction about a married woman who drinks wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between cases of coercion and willingness, or between the wife of a priest and the wife of an Israelite.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between cases of coercion and willingness, or between the wife of a priest and the wife of an Israelite.

items.text: Interpretation of 'And for the one who goes out and comes in there is no peace'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'And for the one who goes out and comes in there is no peace'
items.desc_en: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan each interpret the verse as referring to someone who leaves the study of halakhah for Scripture, Mishnah, or even another Talmudic tractate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'And for the one who goes out and comes in there is no peace' and reports Rav's interpretation that one who leaves a halachic discussion for a biblical reading has no peace.
Shmuel interprets the verse as referring to one who leaves Talmud for Mishnah, and Rabbi Yochanan extends it even to one who leaves one Talmudic discussion for another.
Shmuel interprets the verse as referring to one who leaves Talmud for Mishnah.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse as referring even to one who leaves one Talmudic tractate for another.

items.text: Mishnah: Categories of halakhah with scant Scriptural support
items.text_en: Mishnah: Categories of halakhah with scant Scriptural support
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the annulment of vows has no Scriptural basis, while laws of Shabbat, Chagigah, and me'ilah are like mountains hanging by a hair. Other categories like civil laws and sacrifices have ample Scriptural support.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the laws of annulling vows have no scriptural basis, while the laws of Shabbat, Chagigot, and trespass offerings are like mountains hanging by a hair, and the laws of judgments, Temple service, purity, impurity, and forbidden relations have ample scriptural support.
The Mishnah continues that laws of Shabbat, Chagigah, and me'ilah are like mountains hanging by a hair, with scant Scriptural support but many halakhot.
The Mishnah concludes that civil laws, Temple services, purity and impurity laws, and forbidden relations have ample Scriptural support and are the main body of Torah.

items.text: Tannaitic sources for the annulment of vows
items.text_en: Tannaitic sources for the annulment of vows
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Yitzchak, and Chananyah ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua each cite a verse to prove that the annulment of vows has Scriptural support.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that the annulment of vows has scriptural support from the double occurrence of 'כי יפליא' (when one makes a remarkable vow), one for prohibition and one for permission.
Rabbi Yehoshua argues that the annulment of vows has scriptural support from the verse 'אשר נשבעתי באפי' (I swore in My anger), implying that God can retract His oath.
Rabbi Yitzchak and Chananya ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua each provide additional scriptural support for the annulment of vows from verses about freewill offerings and swearing to keep God's statutes.

Chananyah ben Achi Rabbi Yehoshua cites the verse 'נשבעתי ואקיימה לשמור משפטי צדקך' (I have sworn and I will fulfill it, to keep Your righteous ordinances) to prove that annulment of vows has Scriptural support.

items.text: Samuel's proof is superior and defended by Rava
items.text_en: Samuel's proof is superior and defended by Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah cites Samuel's proof from 'lo yachel devaro' that others may annul his vow. Rava declares that all other proofs have refutations except Samuel's, and then demonstrates the refutations for each. The section concludes with a folk saying praising a sharp pepper over a basket of pumpkins.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah cites Shmuel's proof from the verse 'לֹא יַחֵל דְּבָרוֹ' (he shall not profane his word) that while the vow-maker cannot annul his own vow, others may annul it for him.
Rava declares that all other proofs for the annulment of vows have refutations, except for Shmuel's proof which is unassailable.

sub.text: Rava's refutation of Rabbi Eliezer's proof
sub.text_en: Rava's refutation of Rabbi Eliezer's proof
sub.desc_en: Rava refutes Rabbi Eliezer's proof by suggesting it aligns with Rabbi Yehudah citing Rabbi Tarfon, who holds that nazirite vows are only for the purpose of הפלאה (distinguishing/separating), not for annulment.

sub.text: Rava's refutation of Rabbi Yehoshua's proof
sub.text_en: Rava's refutation of Rabbi Yehoshua's proof
sub.desc_en: Rava refutes Rabbi Yehoshua's proof by suggesting the verse 'בְּאַפִּי נִשְׁבַּעְתִּי' (in My anger I swore) might mean God swore in anger and did not retract, thus not supporting annulment.

sub.text: Rava's refutation of Rabbi Yitzchak's proof
sub.text_en: Rava's refutation of Rabbi Yitzchak's proof
sub.desc_en: Rava refutes Rabbi Yitzchak's proof by suggesting it comes to exclude Shmuel's view that a mental resolve requires verbal expression, not to support annulment.
Rava refutes Chananyah's proof by suggesting it aligns with Rav Giddel citing Rav, who derives that one may swear to fulfill a מצוה (commandment), not that vows can be annulled.
Rava (or alternatively Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak) concludes that Shmuel's proof indeed has no refutation, and cites a folk saying: 'One sharp pepper is better than a basket of pumpkins.'

items.text: Clarification of 'laws of Shabbat' and 'mountains hanging by a hair'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'laws of Shabbat' and 'mountains hanging by a hair'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Shabbat laws are considered scant in Scripture, and answers with Rabbi Abba's case of digging a pit for its dirt. It then explains the phrase 'like mountains hanging by a hair' by noting that the Mishnah's examples are detailed laws derived from scant verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Shabbat laws can be considered 'scant in Scripture' when they are explicitly written in the Torah.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to the detailed halachic derivations, not the explicit verses, and introduces Rabbi Abba's case.
Rabbi Abba states that one who digs a pit on שבת (the Sabbath) only needing its dirt is פטור (exempt) from a sin-offering, a law derived from scant verses.
The Gemara asks which Tanna's opinion Rabbi Abba's ruling aligns with, suggesting it follows Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara answers that it follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds that a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה (unintended labor) is פטור (exempt).
The Gemara objects that even according to Rabbi Yehudah, who normally holds one liable for unintended labor, here the digger is destroying (מקלקל) and thus exempt.
The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'like mountains hanging by a hair'.

items.text: Opening statement: The principle of מלאכת מחשבת
items.text_en: Opening statement: The principle of מלאכת מחשבת
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the concept that the Torah prohibits only intentional work (מלאכת מחשבת), but notes that this principle is not explicitly written in the Torah, setting up the discussion of 'mountains hanging by a hair'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the Torah prohibits only intentional work (מלאכת מחשבת), yet this principle is not explicitly written in the Torah.

items.text: First case: Derivation of Chagigah from the wilderness
items.text_en: First case: Derivation of Chagigah from the wilderness
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the word 'וְחַגּוֹתֶם' refers to sacrifice or just celebration. Through a series of proofs and counter-proofs, it concludes via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'מִדְבָּר' that it means sacrifices, but notes that this derivation is weak because Torah matters cannot be derived from Prophets (דברי תורה מדברי קבלה לא ילפינן).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that the laws of Chagigah are written explicitly, so why is it listed among 'mountains hanging by a hair'? It then introduces Rav Pappa's question to Abaye.
Rav Pappa questions Abaye: how do we know that the verse 'וְחַגּוֹתֶם אוֹתוֹ חַג לַה׳' refers to sacrifice (זְבִיחָה) and not merely to celebrating a festival (חוֹגּוּ חַגָּא)?
The Gemara argues from the verse 'וְיָחוֹגּוּ לִי בַּמִּדְבָּר' that it must mean sacrifices, because Moses explicitly asked for 'זְבָחִים וְעוֹלוֹת' (sacrifices and burnt offerings).

The Gemara objects: perhaps the verse means 'eat, drink, and celebrate before Me'? But it rejects this because the verse 'וְלֹא יָלִין חֵלֶב חַגִּי עַד בֹּקֶר' implies a sacrifice (חֵלֶב, fat) that cannot remain overnight, which would not apply to mere celebration.

The Gemara objects further: perhaps the verse 'חֵלֶב חַגִּי' means fat that comes during the festival, but the general rule 'כׇּל הַלַּיְלָה עַד הַבֹּקֶר' (all night until morning) applies to all sacrifices, so the specific verse is redundant.
The Gemara objects that the general verse might be for a positive commandment (עשה), while the specific verse adds a prohibition (לאו), but another verse already provides a prohibition.
The Gemara objects that the additional verse might be to violate two prohibitions and a positive commandment, not to prove the meaning of 'חַג'.

The Gemara resolves by a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'מִדְבָּר' (wilderness): just as in the verse 'הַזְּבָחִים וּמִנְחָה הִגַּשְׁתֶּם לִי בַּמִּדְבָּר' it means sacrifices, so too here 'וְיָחוֹגּוּ לִי בַּמִּדְבָּר' means sacrifices.

sub.text: Gemara's note on the weakness of the derivation
sub.text_en: Gemara's note on the weakness of the derivation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this derivation is like 'mountains hanging by a hair' because we do not derive Torah laws from Prophetic writings (דברי תורה מדברי קבלה לא ילפינן).

items.text: Transition: The principle of 'mountains hanging by a hair'
items.text_en: Transition: The principle of 'mountains hanging by a hair'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explicitly identifies the first case as an example of 'mountains hanging by a hair' (כַּהֲרָרִין הַתְּלוּיִין בִּשְׂעָרָה), because the derivation relies on a weak link between Torah and Prophets.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the first case as an example of 'mountains hanging by a hair' (כַּהֲרָרִין הַתְּלוּיִין בִּשְׂעָרָה), because the derivation relies on a weak link between Torah and Prophets.

items.text: Second case: Me'ilah and agency
items.text_en: Second case: Me'ilah and agency
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Mishnah about Me'ilah where an agent who fulfills his mission causes the homeowner to be liable, but if not, the agent is liable. This seems contradictory, as one person sins and another is punished, which is another example of 'mountains hanging by a hair'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the laws of Me'ilah are explicitly written in the Torah, so why would they be considered 'mountains hanging by a hair'?
Rami bar Chama explains that the difficulty is not with the written law but with a Mishnah where an agent who fulfills his mission makes the homeowner liable, but if not, the agent is liable.

The Gemara objects that if the agent fulfilled his mission, why should the homeowner be liable? This seems like one person sins and another is punished, which is exactly the phenomenon of 'mountains hanging by a hair'.

items.text: Rava's first answer: Derivation from Terumah
items.text_en: Rava's first answer: Derivation from Terumah
items.desc_en: Rava suggests that the law of Me'ilah is derived from Terumah via a verbal analogy (חֵטְא חֵטְא), where an agent is considered like the principal, so the difficulty is resolved.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges the difficulty raised about the law of Me'ilah, asking what the problem is.
Rava answers that Me'ilah is different because it derives from Terumah via a verbal analogy (חֵטְא חֵטְא), where an agent is considered like the principal, resolving the difficulty.

items.text: Rava's second answer: Case of forgetfulness
items.text_en: Rava's second answer: Case of forgetfulness
items.desc_en: Rava presents a different Mishnah where the homeowner forgot and the agent did not, yet the agent is liable, which is puzzling and exemplifies 'mountains hanging by a hair'.

sub.desc_en: Rava presents a different Mishnah where the homeowner forgot and the agent did not, yet the agent is liable, which is puzzling and exemplifies 'mountains hanging by a hair'.

items.text: Rav Ashi's first answer: Misappropriation of sacred funds
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's first answer: Misappropriation of sacred funds
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi questions the difficulty, suggesting that the agent's action is considered misappropriating sacred funds for secular use, so liability is logical.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi questions the difficulty, suggesting that the agent's action is considered misappropriating sacred funds for secular use, so liability is logical.

items.text: Rav Ashi's second answer: Case of taking a stone or beam
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's second answer: Case of taking a stone or beam
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi presents a Mishnah where one takes a sacred stone or beam and gives it to another, yet only the first is liable, which is puzzling. He suggests it follows Shmuel's principle, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi introduces a Mishnah about taking a sacred stone or beam, where only the first taker is liable, which seems paradoxical.
The gemara questions why the first taker is liable but the second is not, calling it a 'mountain hanging by a hair'.
Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by suggesting the Mishnah follows Shmuel's principle, though the text is cut off.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the mishnah's case of a treasurer
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the mishnah's case of a treasurer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah's ruling about building a house with consecrated materials, suggesting it is like 'mountains hanging by a hair' (a difficulty). It considers Rav's explanation that the case involves placing the stone on a skylight, and then resolves the issue with Rava's approach that the person should have been aware of the consecrated money.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the mishnah's case involves a treasurer to whom consecrated stones were entrusted, so the stone is always in his domain.

The Gemara objects based on the latter clause of the mishnah: if one built the stone into his house, he is not liable until he dwells under it, which seems illogical and like 'mountains hanging by a hair'.
Rav answers that the case is where he placed the stone over a skylight, so dwelling under it is the benefit that triggers misuse.
Rava resolves that the halakha is indeed like 'mountains hanging by a hair' because here the agent did not know about the consecrated money, unlike the case where one should have examined.

items.text: The principle of scant verse with many laws: negaim and ohalot
items.text_en: The principle of scant verse with many laws: negaim and ohalot
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that negaim and ohalot have a scant verse but many laws. Rav Pappa clarifies that negaim actually has a full verse but few laws, while ohalot has a scant verse and many laws. The practical difference is that for doubts in negaim one should examine the verse, for ohalot one should examine the mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle that some topics have a scant verse but many laws.
A baraita is cited stating that the laws of negaim (leprosy) and ohalot (tent impurity) have a scant verse but many laws.
The Gemara objects that negaim actually has a full verse, not a scant one.
Rav Pappa resolves the objection by clarifying that the baraita means negaim has a full verse but few laws, while ohalot has a scant verse and many laws.
The Gemara asks what practical difference this distinction makes.
The Gemara answers that for doubts in negaim one should examine the verse, while for ohalot one should examine the mishnah.

items.text: Dinim (monetary laws) are written in the verse, but needed for Rabbi's derivation
items.text_en: Dinim (monetary laws) are written in the verse, but needed for Rabbi's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why dinim are listed if they are written in the verse, and answers that it is needed for Rabbi's teaching that 'a soul for a soul' refers to monetary compensation, derived from a verbal analogy of 'giving'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why dinim (monetary laws) are listed in the Mishnah's list of topics, since they are already written explicitly in the Torah.
The Gemara answers that the mention of dinim is needed only for Rabbi's teaching, which derives monetary compensation from the verse 'a soul for a soul'.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi says that 'a soul for a soul' refers to monetary compensation, derived via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'giving' used above.

items.text: Avodot (temple services) are written, but needed for the law of carrying the blood
items.text_en: Avodot (temple services) are written, but needed for the law of carrying the blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why avodot are listed if written, and answers it is needed for the law of carrying the blood, which is derived from the verse 'and he shall bring' (holakhah). It concludes that carrying is not excluded from the category of receiving.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why avodot (temple services) are listed in the Mishnah if they are already written in the Torah, and answers that they are needed for the law of carrying the blood (הולכת הדם).

A baraita is cited: the verse 'והקריבו' (and they shall offer) refers to receiving the blood, and the verse 'והקריב הכהן את הכל' (the priest shall offer all) refers to carrying the limbs to the altar ramp, showing that carrying is a distinct service derived from the Torah.
The Gemara concludes that carrying the blood is not excluded from the category of receiving, meaning it is a necessary service that must be listed separately.

items.text: Taharot (purifications) are written, but needed for the measure of a mikveh
items.text_en: Taharot (purifications) are written, but needed for the measure of a mikveh
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why taharot are listed if written, and answers it is needed for the measure of a mikveh (forty se'ah), which is not written in the verse but derived from the requirement that water cover the entire body.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists 'Taharot' (purifications) since they are already written in the Torah.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's listing is needed to teach the measure of a mikveh (forty se'ah), which is not explicitly written in the Torah but derived from the requirement that water cover the entire body.

items.text: Temeot (impurities) are written, but needed for the size of a creeping thing
items.text_en: Temeot (impurities) are written, but needed for the size of a creeping thing
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why temeot are listed if written, and answers it is needed for the size of a creeping thing (ke'adashah), which is not written. The derivation is from the verses 'in them' and 'from them', and the sages set the measure as a lentil, while Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says like the tail of a lizard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the section on impurities (טְמָאוֹת) is listed in the Mishnah if the laws are already written in the Torah, and answers that it is needed for the size of a creeping thing (כַּעֲדָשָׁה), which is not explicitly written.
A baraita is cited that derives from the verses 'בָּהֶם' (in them) and 'מֵהֶם' (from them) that impurity requires a minimum size that is part of the whole but not the whole.
The sages set the measure of impurity for a creeping thing as the size of a lentil (כַּעֲדָשָׁה), because that is the initial size of a snail (חוֹמֶט).

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's opinion
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's opinion
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda argues that the minimum size is like the tail of a lizard (כִּזְנַב הַלְּטָאָה), not a lentil.

items.text: Arayot (forbidden relations) are written, but needed for further derivation (incomplete)
items.text_en: Arayot (forbidden relations) are written, but needed for further derivation (incomplete)
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to ask about arayot, noting they are written, but the text cuts off. This section likely continues the pattern of explaining why arayot are listed despite being written in the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about arayot (forbidden relations), noting that they are already written in the Torah, implying a need for further derivation.

items.text: Conclusion of previous Mishnah: derivation of the prohibition on a daughter from an raped woman
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous Mishnah: derivation of the prohibition on a daughter from an raped woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes a previous discussion by citing Rava's tradition from Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi that the prohibition on a daughter from an raped woman is derived through a verbal analogy of 'henna' and 'zimah'. It then clarifies that both sets of forbidden relations are considered 'bodies of Torah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the topic of the prohibition on a daughter from an raped woman, which is not explicitly written in the Torah.

sub.text: Rava citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi
sub.text_en: Rava citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi
sub.desc_en: Rava reports a tradition from Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi that the prohibition is derived through a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of the word 'henna'.
Rava adds that the derivation also uses a verbal analogy of the word 'zimah'.
The Gemara clarifies that both sets of forbidden relations (the explicit ones and the derived one) are considered 'bodies of Torah' (גופי תורה), meaning fundamental Torah laws.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: restrictions on public study
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: restrictions on public study
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not expound on forbidden relations with three, on the Work of Creation with two, nor on the Chariot with one, unless he is wise and understands on his own. It adds that one who speculates on four things (what is above, below, before, and after) would be better off not having been born.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the restrictions on public study of forbidden relations, the Work of Creation, and the Chariot, and warns against speculating on four forbidden topics.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes an apparent contradiction: the Mishnah first says 'not with one' and then says 'unless he is wise and understands on his own'. It resolves this by explaining that the Mishnah means: one does not expound on forbidden relations with three, on Creation with two, and on the Chariot with one, unless he is wise and understands on his own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an apparent contradiction in the Mishnah: it first says one may not expound the Chariot with one, then says unless he is wise and understands on his own.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah means: one does not expound forbidden relations with three, Creation with two, and the Chariot with one, unless he is wise and understands on his own.

items.text: Reason for the prohibition on studying forbidden relations with three
items.text_en: Reason for the prohibition on studying forbidden relations with three
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the reason why forbidden relations may not be expounded with three. It first suggests a scriptural derivation from 'Ish Ish' and 'She'er Besaro', but is refuted because the same derivation would apply to other prohibitions. It then suggests another derivation from 'Ushmartem et Mishmarti', but is again refuted. Rav Ashi explains that the prohibition is based on logic: with three, one student may discuss with another and they might permit a forbidden relation. The Gemara distinguishes forbidden relations from other areas due to the strong desire, and further distinguishes them from theft.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason why forbidden relations may not be expounded with three.
The Gemara suggests a scriptural derivation from the double expression 'איש איש' (ish ish) and 'שאר בשרו' (she'er besaro) to limit teaching to two.
The Gemara objects that the same derivation would apply to other prohibitions like cursing God or idol worship.
The Gemara answers that those instances of 'איש איש' are needed to include gentiles in the prohibitions.
The Gemara objects that the same inclusion of gentiles applies to forbidden relations as well, so the derivation is not unique.
The Gemara suggests another derivation from 'ושמרתם את משמרתי' (ushmartem et mishmarti) to limit teaching to two.
The Gemara objects that the same derivation would apply to Shabbat, matzot, and sacred things.
Rav Ashi explains that the prohibition applies only to the concealed laws of forbidden relations, not to all aspects.
Rav Ashi explains the logical reason: with three, two students may discuss among themselves and mistakenly permit a forbidden relation.
The Gemara objects that the same logic would apply to all Torah study.
The Gemara distinguishes forbidden relations because the soul covets and lusts after them.
The Gemara objects that theft also involves desire.
The Gemara distinguishes: the inclination for forbidden relations is strong both in presence and absence, while for theft it is strong only when the object is present.

items.text: Source for the prohibition on studying Creation with two
items.text_en: Source for the prohibition on studying Creation with two
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the prohibition on studying the Work of Creation with two from a baraita on the verse 'Ki She'al Na Leyamim Rishonim'. It teaches that one may ask, but not two; one may not ask about what was before Creation; one may ask about the six days of Creation; and one may not ask about what is above, below, before, or after.

items.text: גודלו של אדם הראשון
items.text_en: The dimensions of Adam and the resolution of verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why two verses are needed to describe Adam's creation. Rabbi Elazar and Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav offer different interpretations: Adam was created from earth to the firmament, or from one end of the world to the other. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by stating both verses refer to the same measurement.
items.desc: הגמרא דורשת את הפסוק 'למן היום אשר ברא אלהים אדם על הארץ ולמקצה השמים ועד קצה השמים' ללמד על גודלו של אדם הראשון: לפי רבי אלעזר היה מן הארץ עד הרקיע, ולפי רב יהודה אמר רב היה מסוף העולם ועד סופו. לאחר שחטא מיעטו הקב"ה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why two verses are needed to describe Adam's creation, given that one verse already implies his vast dimensions.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מאחר שכבר דרשנו את הפסוק 'למקצה השמים ועד קצה השמים', למה לי הפסוק 'למן היום אשר ברא אלהים אדם על הארץ'?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that Adam was created from earth to the firmament, and after sinning God diminished him.
sub.desc: רבי אלעזר דורש את הפסוק ללמד שאדם הראשון היה בגובה מן הארץ עד הרקיע, ולאחר שחטא מיעטו הקב"ה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says Adam was created from one end of the world to the other, and after sinning God diminished him.
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב דורש את הפסוק שאדם הראשון היה באורך מסוף העולם ועד סופו, ולאחר שחטא מיעטו הקב"ה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between the two verses by stating that both refer to the same measurement.
sub.desc: הגמרא מיישבת את הסתירה בין הדרשות: שני הפסוקים מלמדים על אותו שיעור, שכן גובהו של אדם הראשון מן הארץ עד הרקיע שווה לאורכו מסוף העולם ועד סופו.

items.text: עשרה דברים שנבראו ביום ראשון
items.text_en: Ten things created on the first day
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav lists ten things created on the first day: heaven and earth, chaos and void, light and darkness, wind and water, and the measure of day and night. Each is supported by a biblical verse. A baraita elaborates on the nature of chaos (tohu) and void (bohu).
items.desc: רב יהודה אמר רב מונה עשרה דברים שנבראו ביום ראשון: שמים וארץ, תהו ובהו, אור וחושך, רוח ומים, מדת יום ומדת לילה. הגמרא מביאה מקורות לכל אחד, ומבארת את תהו ובהו: תהו הוא קו ירוק המקיף את העולם שממנו יצא חושך, ובהו הם אבנים מפולמות משוקעות בתהום שמהן יוצאים מים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav lists ten things created on the first day: heaven, earth, chaos, void, light, darkness, wind, water, and the measure of day and night.
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב מונה עשרה דברים שנבראו ביום ראשון.

sub.desc_en: Each of the ten items is supported by a biblical verse from the creation account.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה מקראות לכל אחד מעשרת הדברים.

sub.desc_en: A baraita elaborates on the nature of chaos (תֹהוּ) as a green line surrounding the world from which darkness emerged, and void (בֹהוּ) as submerged stones in the deep from which water emerges.
sub.desc: ברייתא מבארת את תהו ובהו: תהו הוא קו ירוק המקיף העולם שממנו יצא חושך, ובהו אבנים משוקעות בתהום שמהן יוצאים מים.

items.text: האור הגנוז לצדיקים
items.text_en: The primordial light and its concealment
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how light was created on the first day if the luminaries were set on the fourth day. Rabbi Elazar explains that the light created on the first day allowed Adam to see from one end of the world to the other, but God hid it for the righteous in the future. A baraita records a dispute between Rabbi Yaakov and the Sages: Rabbi Yaakov agrees with Rabbi Elazar, while the Sages say these are the same luminaries that were created on the first day but only suspended on the fourth.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האור נברא ביום ראשון? הרי המאורות נתלו ביום רביעי! מתרץ רבי אלעזר: האור שנברא ביום ראשון היה אור מיוחד שאדם צופה בו מסוף העולם ועד סופו, אך הקב"ה גנזו לצדיקים לעתיד לבוא מפני דור המבול ודור הפלגה. מחלוקת תנאים: רבי יעקב אומר שזה אור מיוחד, וחכמים אומרים שהם המאורות עצמם שנוצרו ביום ראשון אך לא נתלו עד יום רביעי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how light could have been created on the first day if the luminaries were only set on the fourth day.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האור נברא ביום ראשון? הרי המאורות נתלו ביום רביעי.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that the light created on the first day was a special light that allowed Adam to see from one end of the world to the other, but God hid it after seeing the corrupt generations.
sub.desc: רבי אלעזר מתרץ: האור שנברא ביום ראשון היה אור מיוחד שאדם צופה בו מסוף העולם ועד סופו, אך הקב"ה גנזו מפני דור המבול ודור הפלגה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar adds that the light was hidden for the righteous in the future, as implied by the verse 'for the light is good' and 'good' refers to the righteous.
sub.desc: רבי אלעזר מביא ראיה שהאור נגנז לצדיקים לעתיד לבוא, שנאמר 'וירא אלהים את האור כי טוב' ואין טוב אלא צדיק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds that when God saw the light hidden for the righteous, He rejoiced, as it says 'the light of the righteous rejoices.'
sub.desc: רבי אלעזר מביא ראיה נוספת שהאור שמח על שגנזו לצדיקים, שנאמר 'אור צדיקים ישמח'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Yaakov agrees with Rabbi Elazar that the light allowed vision from one end of the world to the other, while the Sages say these are the same luminaries created on the first day but only suspended on the fourth.
sub.desc: ברייתא מביאה מחלוקת תנאים: רבי יעקב אומר שהאור היה מיוחד שאדם צופה בו מסוף העולם ועד סופו.

items.text: Ten things with which the world was created
items.text_en: Ten things with which the world was created
items.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav lists ten attributes through which the world was created: wisdom, understanding, knowledge, strength, rebuke, might, righteousness, justice, kindness, and mercy. Each is supported by a biblical verse.

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviya said Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya said Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav lists ten attributes through which the world was created.
Each of the ten attributes is supported by a biblical verse.

items.text: The expansion of the world and the sea
items.text_en: The expansion of the world and the sea
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav describes how the world initially expanded like two threads of a warp until God rebuked it and stopped it. Resh Lakish connects this to the name 'Shaddai' and also describes how the sea expanded until God rebuked and dried it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav describes how the world initially expanded like two threads of a warp until God rebuked it and stopped it, and Resh Lakish connects this to the name 'Shaddai'.
Resh Lakish adds a parallel description of how the sea expanded until God rebuked and dried it, citing a verse.

items.text: מחלוקת בית שמאי ובית הלל בסדר בריאת שמים וארץ
items.text_en: The order of creation: heaven and earth
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel: Beit Shammai says heaven was created first, Beit Hillel says earth was created first. They argue using analogies and verses. The Sages say both were created simultaneously. Resh Lakish resolves the apparent contradiction between verses: when created, heaven came first; when spread out, earth came first.
items.desc: בית שמאי אומרים שמים נבראו תחילה ואחר כך ארץ, ובית הלל אומרים ארץ נבראה תחילה. כל אחד מביא ראיה מפסוק. חכמים אומרים שניהם נבראו כאחת. ריש לקיש מתרץ: בבריאה נבראו שמים תחילה, אך בנטייה נטה הארץ תחילה.

sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai states that heaven was created first, citing the verse 'בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ' (In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth).
sub.desc: הברייתא מציגה את מחלוקת בית שמאי ובית הלל: בית שמאי אומרים שמים נבראו תחילה, ובית הלל אומרים ארץ נבראה תחילה, כל אחד מביא ראיה מפסוק.

sub.desc_en: Beit Hillel counters that earth was created first, citing the verse 'ביום עשות ה' אלהים ארץ ושמים' (on the day the Lord God made earth and heaven).
sub.desc: הברייתא מציגה את מחלוקת בית שמאי ובית הלל: בית שמאי אומרים שמים נבראו תחילה, ובית הלל אומרים ארץ נבראה תחילה, כל אחד מביא ראיה מפסוק.

sub.text_en: Beit Hillel's objection to Beit Shammai
sub.desc_en: Beit Hillel objects with an analogy: a person builds an upper story only after building the house, citing the verse 'הבונה בשמים מעלותיו ואגודתו על ארץ יסדה' (He who builds His upper chambers in the heavens and founds His bundle on the earth).
sub.desc: בית הלל מקשים על בית שמאי ממשל של בניין עלייה ואחר כך בית, ומביאים ראיה מפסוק באמוס.

sub.text_en: Beit Shammai's objection to Beit Hillel
sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai objects with a counter-analogy: a person makes a footstool before making a throne, citing the verse 'השמים כסאי והארץ הדום רגלי' (the heavens are My throne and the earth My footstool).
sub.desc: בית הלל מקשים על בית שמאי ממשל של בניין עלייה ואחר כך בית, ומביאים ראיה מפסוק באמוס.

sub.desc_en: The Sages resolve the dispute by stating that both heaven and earth were created simultaneously, citing the verse 'אף ידי יסדה ארץ וימיני טפחה שמים קורא אני אליהם יעמדו יחדו' (My hand laid the foundation of the earth, and My right hand spread out the heavens; I call to them, they stand together).
sub.desc: בית הלל מקשים על בית שמאי ממשל של בניין עלייה ואחר כך בית, ומביאים ראיה מפסוק באמוס.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'יחדו' (together) in the Sages' verse, and explains that it means they are inseparable from each other.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: לדעת חכמים, מה פירוש 'יחדיו'? ומתרצת: שאינם נפרדים זה מזה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verses cited by Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel contradict each other.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: לדעת חכמים, מה פירוש 'יחדיו'? ומתרצת: שאינם נפרדים זה מזה.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish resolves the contradiction: when created, heaven came first; when spread out, earth came first.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: לדעת חכמים, מה פירוש 'יחדיו'? ומתרצת: שאינם נפרדים זה מזה.

items.text: משמעות המילה 'שמים'
items.text_en: The meaning of 'shamayim' and the exegesis of 'et'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains 'shamayim' as 'there is water' (sham mayim). A baraita teaches that God brought fire and water and mixed them to make the firmament. Rabbi Yishmael asks Rabbi Akiva what Nachum Ish Gamzu derived from the word 'et' in 'et hashamayim ve'et ha'aretz'. Rabbi Akiva explains that without 'et', one might think 'shamayim' refers to God's name, but with 'et', it means the actual heaven and earth.
items.desc: רבי יוסי בר חנינא אומר: 'שמים' – שם מים. בברייתא: אש ומים, שהקב"ה טרפם זה בזה ועשה מהם רקיע. רבי ישמעאל שואל את רבי עקיבא על דרשת נחום איש גמזו ב'את השמים ואת הארץ', ורבי עקיבא משיב שאלמלא 'את' היה נדרש ששמים וארץ הם שמותיו של הקב"ה, אך עם 'את' הכוונה לשמים וארץ ממש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'shamayim' means.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת על משמעות המילה 'שמים', ורבי יוסי בר חנינא עונה שהיא ראשי תיבות של 'שם מים'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains that 'shamayim' means 'there is water' (שם מים).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת על משמעות המילה 'שמים', ורבי יוסי בר חנינא עונה שהיא ראשי תיבות של 'שם מים'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that God brought fire and water and mixed them to make the firmament.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת על משמעות המילה 'שמים', ורבי יוסי בר חנינא עונה שהיא ראשי תיבות של 'שם מים'.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's question to Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael asks Rabbi Akiva what Nachum Ish Gamzu derived from the word 'et' in the verse 'et hashamayim ve'et ha'aretz'.
sub.desc: רבי ישמעאל שואל את רבי עקיבא כיצד נחום איש גמזו דרש את המילה 'את' בפסוק 'את השמים ואת הארץ'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva explains that without 'et', one might think 'shamayim' refers to God's name, but with 'et', it means the actual heaven and earth.
sub.desc: רבי ישמעאל שואל את רבי עקיבא כיצד נחום איש גמזו דרש את המילה 'את' בפסוק 'את השמים ואת הארץ'.

items.text: Opening question on the order of creation
items.text_en: Opening question on the order of creation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah mentions the earth before the heavens in the verse 'and the earth was formless and void,' given that creation began with heaven. A baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael offers a parable of a king who praises those who rise early for him, even if it is not their custom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah mentions the earth before the heavens in the verse 'וְהָאָרֶץ הָיְתָה תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ' (and the earth was formless and void), given that creation began with heaven.

The school of Rabbi Yishmael answers with a parable of a king who praises those who rise early for him, even if it is not their custom, explaining why the earth is mentioned first despite being created later.

items.text: Foundations of the earth
items.text_en: Foundations of the earth
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei laments that people do not understand what they see. He explains that the earth stands on pillars, which stand on water, which stands on mountains, which stand on wind, which stands on a storm, which is suspended from God's arm. The Sages say the earth stands on twelve pillars, others say seven, and Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua says it stands on one pillar named 'Righteous.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei laments that people see and stand without understanding what they see or what they stand on.

Rabbi Yosei explains that the earth stands on pillars, which stand on water, which stand on mountains, which stand on wind, which stand on a storm, which is suspended from God's arm, each supported by a verse.
The Sages say the earth stands on twelve pillars, citing a verse about the boundaries of the nations.
Some say the earth stands on seven pillars, citing a verse about wisdom's pillars.
Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua says the earth stands on one pillar named 'Righteous,' citing the verse 'and the righteous is the foundation of the world.'

items.text: Number of heavens: two
items.text_en: Number of heavens: two
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that there are two heavens, citing the verse 'the heavens and the heaven of heavens.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that there are two heavens (רקיעים), citing the verse 'the heavens and the heaven of heavens.'

items.text: Seven heavens and their contents
items.text_en: Seven heavens and their contents
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish enumerates seven heavens: Vilon, Rakia, Shechakim, Zevul, Ma'on, Machon, and Aravot. Each heaven is described with its contents and scriptural proofs. The section includes details about the heavenly Jerusalem, the ministering angels, storehouses of snow and hail, and the presence of the Divine throne.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish opens by stating that there are seven heavens and lists their names: Vilon, Rakia, Shechakim, Zevul, Ma'on, Machon, and Aravot.
Resh Lakish describes Vilon as a curtain that serves no other purpose than to enter at morning and exit at evening, renewing the work of creation daily, and cites a verse.
Resh Lakish describes Rakia as the firmament in which the sun, moon, stars, and constellations are fixed, citing a verse.
Resh Lakish describes Shechakim as containing millstones that grind manna for the righteous, citing a verse.
Resh Lakish describes Zevul as containing the heavenly Jerusalem and Temple with Michael the great prince offering sacrifices, and proves it is called heaven from a verse.
Resh Lakish describes Ma'on as containing groups of ministering angels who sing at night and are silent by day for Israel's honor, citing a verse.

sub.text: Resh Lakish's homily on Torah study at night
sub.text_en: Resh Lakish's homily on Torah study at night
sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish digresses to teach that one who engages in Torah at night receives a thread of kindness by day, citing the same verse; an alternative version applies this to the World to Come.
Rabbi Levi adds that one who stops Torah study for idle talk is fed coals of broom, and proves Ma'on is called heaven from a verse.
Resh Lakish describes Machon as containing storehouses of snow, hail, harmful dew, chambers of storm and cave of steam, with doors of fire, citing a verse.
The Gemara objects that these storehouses of snow, hail, etc. are described in a verse as being on earth, not in heaven.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers that David prayed for mercy and brought them down to earth, citing a verse, and proves Machon is called heaven.

Resh Lakish describes Aravot as containing justice, judgment, righteousness, treasures of life, peace, blessing, souls of the righteous, souls yet to be created, and the dew of resurrection, each with a verse.
Resh Lakish provides additional scriptural proofs for the souls of the righteous, souls yet to be created, and the dew of resurrection in Aravot.

Resh Lakish concludes that Aravot contains the ofanim, seraphim, holy creatures, ministering angels, and the Divine throne, proving it is called heaven through a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'riding'.

items.text: Darkness surrounding God
items.text_en: Darkness surrounding God
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that darkness, cloud, and fog surround God, citing a verse. It then raises a contradiction: is there darkness before God, given that light dwells with Him? The Gemara begins to resolve this, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that darkness, cloud, and fog surround God, citing a verse.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: is there darkness before God, given that light dwells with Him?
The Gemara begins to resolve the contradiction, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's addition about the firmament above the Chayot
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's addition about the firmament above the Chayot
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov adds that there is another firmament above the heads of the Chayot, citing the verse 'And over the heads of the Chayot there was a firmament like the awesome ice'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov asserts that there is an additional firmament above the heads of the Chayot, citing the verse 'And over the heads of the Chayot there was a firmament like the awesome ice'.

items.text: The limit of inquiry and the Bat Kol's response to the wicked one
items.text_en: The limit of inquiry and the Bat Kol's response to the wicked one
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that one may speak only up to this point, quoting Ben Sira about not delving into the hidden. It then cites a Baraita where Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai describes the Bat Kol's response to the wicked one who sought to ascend to heaven, detailing the vast distances and the hierarchy of creation from earth to the Divine throne.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara declares the limit of permissible inquiry and cites Ben Sira's warning not to delve into the hidden.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai
sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the Bat Kol's response to the wicked one who sought to ascend to heaven.
The Bat Kol details the vast distances from earth to the Divine throne, concluding that the wicked one will be cast down to Sheol.

items.text: The rule of not teaching Ma'aseh Merkavah to an individual
items.text_en: The rule of not teaching Ma'aseh Merkavah to an individual
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Ma'aseh Merkavah is not taught to an individual. Rabbi Chiya teaches that one may transmit chapter headings. Rabbi Zeira adds that chapter headings are only transmitted to the Av Beit Din and to one whose heart is anxious within him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Ma'aseh Merkavah is not taught to an individual.
Rabbi Chiya teaches that one may transmit chapter headings of Ma'aseh Merkavah to an individual.
Rabbi Zeira adds that chapter headings are only transmitted to the Av Beit Din and to one whose heart is anxious within him.

items.text: Rabbi Ami's conditions for transmitting secrets of Torah
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami's conditions for transmitting secrets of Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami states that the secrets of Torah are only transmitted to one who possesses five qualities: a captain of fifty, a man of stature, a counselor, a cunning artisan, and a whisperer. He also says that words of Torah are not transmitted to a gentile.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami states that the secrets of Torah are only transmitted to one who possesses five specific qualities listed in the verse.
Rabbi Ami adds that words of Torah are not transmitted to a gentile, citing the verse that God did not do so for any nation.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's offer to Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Asi's subsequent offer
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's offer to Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Asi's subsequent offer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Rabbi Elazar to come and learn Ma'aseh Merkavah, but Rabbi Elazar declines, saying he is not old enough. After Rabbi Yochanan's death, Rabbi Asi offers to teach Rabbi Elazar, but Rabbi Elazar asks if he had learned it from Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan invites Rabbi Elazar to learn Ma'aseh Merkavah, but Rabbi Elazar declines, saying he is not old enough.
The narrative reports that Rabbi Yochanan subsequently died.
After Rabbi Yochanan's death, Rabbi Asi offers to teach Rabbi Elazar Ma'aseh Merkavah.
Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Asi whether he had learned Ma'aseh Merkavah from Rabbi Yochanan, implying that only a direct student of Rabbi Yochanan is qualified to teach it.

items.text: Rav Yosef and the elders of Pumbedita: teaching Ma'aseh Merkavah after Ma'aseh Bereishit
items.text_en: Rav Yosef and the elders of Pumbedita: teaching Ma'aseh Merkavah after Ma'aseh Bereishit
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef, who had learned Ma'aseh Merkavah, was asked by the elders of Pumbedita to teach them. He first asked them to teach him Ma'aseh Bereishit. After they did, he taught them Ma'aseh Merkavah, citing verses that such matters should be kept hidden. Rabbi Avahu adds a similar teaching from another verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef, who had learned Ma'aseh Merkavah, was asked by the elders of Pumbedita to teach them, but he first asked them to teach him Ma'aseh Bereishit.

After they taught him Ma'aseh Bereishit, Rav Yosef taught them Ma'aseh Merkavah, citing the verse 'דבש וחלב תחת לשונך' (honey and milk under your tongue) to indicate that these matters should be kept hidden.
Rabbi Avahu adds a similar teaching from the verse 'כבשים ללבושך' (lambs for your clothing), meaning matters that are the secrets of the world should be kept under your garment.

sub.text: Elders of Pumbedita and Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Elders of Pumbedita and Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: The elders asked Rav Yosef up to which point they had learned, and he confirmed that the material they covered up to 'ויאמר אלי בן אדם' (and He said to me, son of man) is indeed Ma'aseh Merkavah.

items.text: The extent of Ma'aseh Merkavah: disputes between Rabbi and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.text_en: The extent of Ma'aseh Merkavah: disputes between Rabbi and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Baraita that defines the extent of Ma'aseh Merkavah. Rabbi says up to 'va'ereh' (the second one), Rabbi Yitzchak says up to 'chashmal'. Up to 'va'ereh' we teach fully, beyond that we transmit chapter headings. Alternatively, up to 'va'ereh' we transmit chapter headings, and beyond that, if the student is wise, he understands on his own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that asks: up to where does the study of Ma'aseh Merkavah extend?
Rabbi states that the study extends up to the second occurrence of 'va'ereh'.
Rabbi Yitzchak states that the study extends up to the word 'chashmal'.
One version of the baraita rules: up to 'va'ereh' we teach fully, beyond that we transmit only chapter headings.
An alternative version states: up to 'va'ereh' we transmit chapter headings, and beyond that, if the student is wise he understands on his own, otherwise not.

items.text: Objection from the incident of the child who was burned by fire from Chashmal
items.text_en: Objection from the incident of the child who was burned by fire from Chashmal
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Do we actually expound on Chashmal? There was a child who expounded on Chashmal and fire came out and consumed him! The Gemara answers: A child is different, as his time has not yet come (he is not of age).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Do we actually expound on Chashmal? There was a child who expounded on Chashmal and fire came out and consumed him!
The Gemara answers: A child is different, as his time has not yet come (he is not of age).

items.text: Chananyah ben Chizkiyah saves the book of Yechezkel
items.text_en: Chananyah ben Chizkiyah saves the book of Yechezkel
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah says: Remember that man for good, Chananyah ben Chizkiyah, who saved the book of Yechezkel from being hidden because its words contradicted the Torah. He brought up 300 jugs of oil and sat in an upper chamber and expounded it. The Rabbis taught about a child who was burned by fire from Chashmal while reading Yechezkel, and they sought to hide the book, but Chananyah ben Chizkiyah argued that not everyone is a sage.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah praises Chananyah ben Chizkiyah for saving the book of Yechezkel from being hidden by expounding it in an upper chamber with 300 jugs of oil.
The Rabbis relate a story of a child burned by fire from Chashmal while reading Yechezkel, and Chananyah ben Chizkiyah argues that not everyone is a sage, thus preventing the book's hiding.

items.text: Introduction to the meaning of Chashmal
items.text_en: Introduction to the meaning of Chashmal
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to ask: What is Chashmal? Rav Yehudah starts to answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the meaning of the word 'חַשְׁמַל' (Chashmal)?
Rav Yehudah begins to answer the question about Chashmal.

items.text: The hayyot's speech and silence
items.text_en: The hayyot's speech and silence
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that the hayyot are sometimes silent and sometimes speak: when the divine word issues from the Holy One they are silent, and when it does not they speak.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that the hayyot are sometimes silent and sometimes speak, depending on whether the divine word is issuing from the Holy One.

items.text: Interpretation of 'ratzo vashov' and 'bazak'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'ratzo vashov' and 'bazak'
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains 'ratzo vashov' as like fire from a furnace, and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains 'kemareh habazak' as like fire from between potsherds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'ratzo vashov' (running and returning) in the verse.
Rav Yehuda explains 'ratzo vashov' as like fire emerging from a furnace.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'kemareh habazak' (like the appearance of the bazak).
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains 'kemareh habazak' as like fire emerging from between potsherds.

items.text: The storm wind from the north and Nebuchadnezzar
items.text_en: The storm wind from the north and Nebuchadnezzar
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that the storm wind went to subdue the entire world under Nebuchadnezzar, so that the nations would not say God handed His children over to a lowly nation; God laments that Israel's sins caused Him to serve idolaters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the storm wind went.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that the storm wind went to subdue the entire world under Nebuchadnezzar, so that the nations would not say God handed His children over to a lowly nation; God laments that Israel's sins caused Him to serve idolaters.

items.text: The angel Sandalfon
items.text_en: The angel Sandalfon
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar identifies the 'ofan' as an angel standing on earth with its head reaching the hayyot; a baraita names him Sandalfon, who is 500 years' journey tall, stands behind the chariot, and ties crowns for his Maker. The Gemara questions how he can tie crowns if God's place is unknown, and answers that he recites a name and the crown goes to its place.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse about the 'ofan' as referring to an angel standing on earth with its head reaching the hayyot.
A baraita names the angel Sandalfon, describes his immense height of 500 years' journey, and states that he stands behind the chariot and ties crowns for his Maker.
The Gemara questions how Sandalfon can tie crowns for God if no one knows God's place, as implied by the verse 'ברוך כבוד ה' ממקומו'.
The Gemara answers that Sandalfon recites a Divine name, causing the crown to fly and settle on its proper place.

items.text: Comparison of Ezekiel and Isaiah's visions
items.text_en: Comparison of Ezekiel and Isaiah's visions
items.desc_en: Rava compares Ezekiel to a villager who saw the king and Isaiah to a city-dweller who saw the king.
