Resh Lakish explains the verse 'ashira laHashem ki ga'oh ga'ah' as a song for He who is exalted over the exalted: the king of hayyot is the lion, of beasts the ox, of birds the eagle, and man is exalted over them, and God over all.

sub.desc_en: Rava compares Ezekiel's vision to a villager seeing the king and Isaiah's to a city-dweller seeing the king.
Resh Lakish explains the verse 'ashira laHashem ki ga'oh ga'ah' as a song for He who is exalted over the exalted, listing the kings of hayyot, beasts, birds, man, and God.

items.text: Contradiction in the faces of the hayyot: ox replaced by cherub
items.text_en: Contradiction in the faces of the hayyot: ox replaced by cherub
items.desc_en: One verse lists an ox face, another lists a cherub face instead. Resh Lakish says Ezekiel prayed and turned the ox into a cherub, arguing that a prosecutor should not become a defender.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction: one verse lists an ox face among the hayyot, but another verse lists a cherub face instead of the ox.
Resh Lakish explains that Ezekiel prayed and transformed the ox face into a cherub, arguing that a prosecutor (the ox, recalling the golden calf) should not become a defender.

items.text: Meaning of 'cherub' and distinction from human face
items.text_en: Meaning of 'cherub' and distinction from human face
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains 'cherub' as 'keravya' (like a child) in Babylonian. Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if cherub and human are both mentioned, they seem redundant; Abaye answers: large face vs. small face.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains that 'cherub' (כְּרוּב) means 'like a child' (כְּרָבְיָא), as in Babylonia they call a child 'ravya'.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if the verse lists both 'face of a cherub' and 'face of a man', they seem redundant — what is the difference?
Abaye answers: the cherub face is a large face (אַפֵּי רַבְרְבֵי) and the human face is a small face (אַפֵּי זוּטְרֵי), distinguishing between the two.

items.text: Contradiction in number of wings: six vs. four
items.text_en: Contradiction in number of wings: six vs. four
items.desc_en: One verse says six wings, another says four. The Gemara resolves: when the Temple stood, six; when it was destroyed, four, as if the wings of the hayyot were diminished.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two verses: one says the hayyot have six wings each, the other says four wings each.
The Gemara resolves: the six-winged description applies when the Temple stood, the four-winged when it was destroyed, as if the wings of the hayyot were diminished.

items.text: Which wings were diminished: those for song or for covering feet?
items.text_en: Which wings were diminished: those for song or for covering feet?
items.desc_en: Rav Chananel in Rav's name says the wings used for song were diminished, citing verses. The Rabbis say those covering the feet were diminished, citing 'v'ragleihem regel yeshara'. The Gemara objects: perhaps they were revealed? It answers: it is proper to reveal the face before one's master, but not the feet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which set of wings were diminished: those for song or those for covering the feet.
Rav Chananel in Rav's name answers that the wings used for song were diminished, citing verses about flying and calling.
The Rabbis answer that the wings covering the feet were diminished, citing the verse 'וְרַגְלֵיהֶם רֶגֶל יְשָׁרָה' and rejecting the alternative that they were merely revealed.
The Gemara resolves the objection: revealing the face before one's master is proper, but revealing the feet is not, so the wings must have been diminished.

items.text: Contradiction in the number of angelic hosts
items.text_en: Contradiction in the number of angelic hosts
items.desc_en: One verse says a thousand thousands serve Him, another says His troops have no number. The Gemara resolves: when the Temple stood, the heavenly retinue was diminished; when it was destroyed, it was not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: one verse says a thousand thousands serve Him, another says His troops have no number.
The Gemara resolves: when the Temple stood, the heavenly retinue was diminished; when it was destroyed, it was not.

items.text: Interpretations of 'elef alfin' and the river of fire
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'elef alfin' and the river of fire
items.desc_en: Rabbi in the name of Abba Yosei ben Dosai says 'elef alfin' is the number of one troop, and His troops are countless. Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says 'elef alfin' refers to the river of fire. The Gemara asks where it comes from: from the sweat of the hayyot. Rav Zutra bar Toviya in Rav's name says it pours on the heads of the wicked in Gehinnom; Rav Acha bar Yaakov says on those who were crushed (the 974 generations).

sub.text: Baraita: Rabbi in the name of Abba Yosei ben Dosai
sub.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi in the name of Abba Yosei ben Dosai
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi in the name of Abba Yosei ben Dosai, interpreting 'elef alfin' as the number of one troop, and His troops are countless.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba interprets 'elef alfin' as referring to the river of fire (נהר דינור), citing the verse.
The Gemara asks where the river of fire originates, and answers: from the sweat of the hayyot (חיות).

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in Rav's name
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in Rav's name
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in Rav's name says the river pours on the heads of the wicked in Gehinnom, citing a verse.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov says the river pours on those who were crushed (the 974 generations that were suppressed before creation), citing a verse.
A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon he-Chasid, identifying the 'crushed ones' as the 974 generations that were suppressed before being created.

items.text: Interpretation of 'Kumtu' and the fate of the wicked
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'Kumtu' and the fate of the wicked
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak interprets the verse 'Asher kumtu' as referring to Torah scholars who humble themselves in this world, and God reveals secrets to them in the world to come. This contrasts with the earlier notion that the verse refers to the wicked who were not created.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak interprets the verse 'אשר קמטו' (who are crushed) as a blessing, referring to Torah scholars who humble themselves over Torah in this world, and God reveals secrets to them in the world to come, as the verse says 'נהר יוצק יסודם' (a river pours out their foundation).

items.text: Creation of angels from the river of fire
items.text_en: Creation of angels from the river of fire
items.desc_en: Shmuel tells Chiyya bar Rav that new ministering angels are created daily from the river of fire, sing, and cease. This disagrees with Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, who says each utterance from God creates an angel.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel tells Chiyya bar Rav that new ministering angels are created daily from the river of fire, sing, and cease, citing the verse 'חֲדָשִׁים לַבְּקָרִים רַבָּה אֱמוּנָתֶךָ'.
The gemara notes that this disagrees with Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, who says each utterance from God creates an angel, citing the verse 'בִּדְבַר ה׳ שָׁמַיִם נַעֲשׂוּ וּבְרוּחַ פִּיו כָּל צְבָאָם'.

items.text: Contradiction in God's appearance resolved
items.text_en: Contradiction in God's appearance resolved
items.desc_en: A contradiction between verses describing God's hair as white like wool and black as a raven is resolved: white in judgment (session), black in war. The Gemara cites a principle that an elder is fitting for judgment, a youth for war.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two verses describing God's hair: one says white like wool, the other says black like a raven.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: white hair represents God in judgment (session), black hair represents God in war.
The Gemara cites Mar's principle that an elder is fitting for judgment and a youth is fitting for war, supporting the resolution.

items.text: Two thrones: for judgment and righteousness
items.text_en: Two thrones: for judgment and righteousness
items.desc_en: A contradiction about God's throne of fire and multiple thrones is resolved: one throne for judgment and one for righteousness, according to Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili objects, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya reinterprets: one throne and one footstool.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises a contradiction between two verses: one describes God's throne as fiery, the other mentions multiple thrones.
The gemara resolves that one throne is for God and one for David, citing a baraita.
A baraita is cited: one throne for God and one for David, according to Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili objects to Rabbi Akiva, arguing that making a throne for David profanes the Divine Presence, and instead says one throne is for judgment and one for righteousness.
The gemara asks whether Rabbi Akiva accepted Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's objection.
The gemara brings a baraita to resolve: Rabbi Akiva now says one throne for judgment and one for righteousness, indicating he accepted the objection.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya objects to Rabbi Akiva, telling him to stick to halacha, and reinterprets: one throne and one footstool.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya explains: one throne for sitting and one footstool for God's feet, citing the verse 'השמים כסאי והארץ הדום רגלי'.

items.text: Isaiah's eighteen curses and their interpretation
items.text_en: Isaiah's eighteen curses and their interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Isaiah cursed Israel with eighteen curses, and only calmed down after saying 'the youth will behave insolently against the elder.' The Gemara enumerates the curses from Isaiah 3, interpreting each as referring to different types of Torah scholars and leaders, culminating in the insolence of the ignorant against the learned.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Isaiah cursed Israel with eighteen curses and only calmed down after saying the verse about the youth behaving insolently toward the elder.
The Gemara asks what the eighteen curses are, and cites the verses from Isaiah 3 that enumerate them.
The Gemara interprets 'משען' as referring to masters of Scripture and 'משענה' as masters of Mishnah, with a dispute between Rav Pappa and the Rabbis about the number of Mishnah orders.

The Gemara interprets each term from the verse: 'משען לחם' as masters of Talmud, 'משען מים' as masters of Aggadah, 'גבור' as master of traditions, 'איש מלחמה' as one skilled in Torah debate, 'שופט' as a true judge, 'נביא' literally, 'קוסם' as a king, and 'זקן' as one fit for the academy.

The Gemara interprets 'שר חמישים' as one who can debate the five books of the Torah, and alternatively as a rule that a translator must be at least fifty years old; 'נשוא פנים' is one whose generation is honored for his sake, citing Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa and Rabbi Abahu.

The Gemara interprets 'יועץ' as one who knows intercalation, 'חכם' as a student who makes his teachers wise, 'חרשים' as making all silent when he opens Torah, 'נבון' as one who understands one thing from another, and 'לחש' as one fit to receive Torah given in a whisper.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's interpretation of 'ונתתי נערים שריהם'
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's interpretation of 'ונתתי נערים שריהם'
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that 'ונתתי נערים שריהם' refers to people who are stripped of mitzvot.

sub.text: Rav Pappa bar Yaakov's interpretation and conclusion
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa bar Yaakov's interpretation and conclusion
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa bar Yaakov interprets 'תעלולים' as foxes, sons of foxes, and explains that Isaiah only calmed down when he said the verse about the insolent youth and the despised, referring to those stripped of mitzvot rebelling against those full of mitzvot.

items.text: The faithful in Jerusalem's downfall
items.text_en: The faithful in Jerusalem's downfall
items.desc_en: Rav Katina says even during Jerusalem's downfall, there were faithful people. The Gemara interprets verses about a man refusing leadership due to lack of Torah knowledge, and discusses the excuse of forgetting.

sub.desc_en: Rav Katina asserts that even during Jerusalem's downfall, there were faithful people, citing a verse about a man offering leadership.
The Gemara interprets the verse's phrases: 'יִשָּׂא' as an oath, 'לֹא אֶהְיֶה חוֹבֵשׁ' as not being a Torah scholar, and lack of bread and garment as lacking Scripture, Mishnah, and Gemara.
The Gemara questions whether the man could have excused himself by claiming he forgot his learning, since if he said he learned, they would test him.
The Gemara answers that the man's statement 'לֹא אֶהְיֶה חוֹבֵשׁ' means he was never a Torah scholar at all, so the excuse of forgetting does not apply.

items.text: Contradiction about faithful people in Jerusalem
items.text_en: Contradiction about faithful people in Jerusalem
items.desc_en: A contradiction arises: Rav Katina said faithful people remained, but Rava said Jerusalem was destroyed only when faithful people ceased. The Gemara begins to resolve this, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rav Katina said faithful people never ceased in Jerusalem, but Rava said Jerusalem was destroyed only when faithful people ceased, citing a verse.
The Gemara begins to resolve the contradiction, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Distinction between Torah study and business
items.text_en: Distinction between Torah study and business
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier ruling about not expounding Ma'aseh Merkavah alone applies to Torah study, but not to business dealings (where it is permitted).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between Torah study (where the restriction applies) and business dealings (where it does not).

items.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh's exposition before Rabban Yochanan ben Zakai
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh's exposition before Rabban Yochanan ben Zakai
items.desc_en: A story is told: Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh asks to learn Ma'aseh Merkavah from Rabban Yochanan ben Zakai, who initially demurs. When Rabbi Elazar asks to say something he had been taught, Rabban Yochanan dismounts, wraps himself, and sits under an olive tree. Rabbi Elazar then expounds, fire descends from heaven, trees sing, and an angel affirms the exposition. Rabban Yochanan blesses him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a story: Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh asks Rabban Yochanan ben Zakai to teach him a chapter of Ma'aseh Merkavah; Rabban Yochanan initially refuses, citing the rule against teaching it to an individual, but then permits Rabbi Elazar to say something he had been taught.
Rabban Yochanan dismounts, wraps himself, and sits under an olive tree; Rabbi Elazar expounds Ma'aseh Merkavah, causing fire to descend from heaven and trees to sing.
An angel affirms the exposition, and Rabban Yochanan blesses Rabbi Elazar, praising him as one who both expounds and fulfills the teaching.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yosei the Kohen's exposition and Rabban Yochanan's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yosei the Kohen's exposition and Rabban Yochanan's response
items.desc_en: When the story reaches Rabbi Yehoshua, he and Rabbi Yosei the Kohen decide to expound Ma'aseh Merkavah as well. Rabbi Yehoshua expounds, and a rainbow appears in the clouds. Rabbi Yosei reports to Rabban Yochanan, who blesses them and recounts a dream where a bat kol invites them to a heavenly banquet.

sub.desc_en: When the story reaches Rabbi Yehoshua, he and Rabbi Yosei the Kohen decide to expound Ma'aseh Merkavah as well.
Rabbi Yehoshua expounds, and a rainbow appears in the clouds; ministering angels gather like people to see a wedding celebration.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei the Kohen's report and Rabban Yochanan's response
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei the Kohen's report and Rabban Yochanan's response
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei reports to Rabban Yochanan, who blesses them and recounts a dream where a bat kol invites them to a heavenly banquet.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita listing three expositions
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita listing three expositions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the story: a baraita lists only three expositions (Rabbi Yehoshua before Rabban Yochanan, Rabbi Akiva before Rabbi Yehoshua, Chananya ben Chachinai before Rabbi Akiva), omitting Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh. The Gemara resolves that the baraita counts only those who expounded before their teacher, not those who expounded before someone who was not their teacher, but Chananya ben Chachinai is included because he at least expounded before his teacher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the story by citing a baraita (תניא) of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda that lists only three expositions, omitting Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita counts only those who expounded before their teacher, not before someone who was not their teacher, but Chananya ben Chachinai is included because he at least expounded before his teacher.

items.text: The four who entered the Pardes
items.text_en: The four who entered the Pardes
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that four entered the Pardes: Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, Acher, and Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva warns them not to say 'water, water' when they reach pure marble stones. Ben Azzai died, Ben Zoma was harmed, Acher cut the plantings, and Rabbi Akiva emerged safely.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the four who entered the Pardes: Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, Acher, and Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Akiva warns them not to say 'water, water' when they reach pure marble stones, citing the verse about false speech.
The baraita reports the outcomes: Ben Azzai died, Ben Zoma was harmed, Acher cut the plantings, and Rabbi Akiva emerged safely.

items.text: Halakhic queries to Ben Zoma
items.text_en: Halakhic queries to Ben Zoma
items.desc_en: Ben Zoma is asked two questions: about castrating a dog (he answers based on the verse 'in your land you shall not do') and about a virgin who became pregnant for a High Priest (the Gemara begins to cite Shmuel's concern).

sub.desc_en: The questioners ask Ben Zoma whether it is permitted to castrate a dog, and he answers based on the verse 'ובארצכם לא תעשו' (in your land you shall not do), implying that any act of castration is forbidden in the land.
The questioners ask Ben Zoma about a virgin who became pregnant and whether she is permitted to a High Priest, introducing Shmuel's concern that will be cited.

items.text: Gemara's question about Samuel's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Samuel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one can have multiple acts of intercourse without emitting semen, and whether Samuel's ruling about seed that does not shoot like an arrow is relevant. It concludes that initially it did shoot like an arrow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one can have multiple acts of intercourse without emitting semen, and whether Samuel's ruling about seed that does not shoot like an arrow is relevant, concluding that initially it did shoot like an arrow.
The Gemara answers by citing Samuel's principle that seed which does not shoot like an arrow cannot fertilize, and explains that initially it did shoot like an arrow.

items.text: Story of Ben Zoma and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Story of Ben Zoma and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The Sages recount a story where Ben Zoma was contemplating the space between the upper and lower waters, and Rabbi Yehoshua remarked that Ben Zoma was still outside (of proper understanding).

sub.desc_en: The Sages introduce a story about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya standing on the Temple Mount.
Rabbi Yehoshua sees Ben Zoma not standing before him and asks where he is coming from.
Ben Zoma explains he was contemplating the gap between the upper and lower waters, citing the verse about the spirit hovering like a dove.
Rabbi Yehoshua tells his disciples that Ben Zoma is still outside (of proper understanding).

items.text: Discussion of the separation of waters
items.text_en: Discussion of the separation of waters
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the timing of the separation of waters and the distance between them, citing various opinions about the measurement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Ben Zoma could speak about the separation of waters on the first day, since the separation only occurred on the second day.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the distance between the upper and lower waters is as thin as a hair.
The Sages answer that the distance is like the width of a camel's neck.
Mar Zutra (or alternatively Rav Asi) answers that the distance is like two cloaks spread one on top of the other, or like two cups placed one on top of the other.

items.text: Acher cuts the shoots: seeing Metatron
items.text_en: Acher cuts the shoots: seeing Metatron
items.desc_en: Acher (Elisha ben Avuya) saw Metatron sitting and writing merits, which led him to question whether there are two powers in heaven. As punishment, Metatron was struck and Acher's merits were erased, and a heavenly voice excluded him from repentance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Acher (Elisha ben Avuya) who 'cut the shoots' and cites the verse applied to him.
The Gemara asks what Acher did to deserve this verse.
The Gemara explains that Acher saw Metatron sitting and writing merits, which led him to suspect there are two powers in heaven.
The Gemara describes the punishment: Metatron was struck with sixty lashes of fire, Acher's merits were erased, and a heavenly voice excluded him from repentance.

items.text: Acher's descent into heresy
items.text_en: Acher's descent into heresy
items.desc_en: Acher, despairing of the world to come, decided to enjoy this world. He went out to evil ways, and when a prostitute recognized him, he desecrated the Sabbath to prove he was Acher.

sub.desc_en: Acher decides that since he has been excluded from the World to Come, he will enjoy this world.
Acher goes out to evil ways, encounters a prostitute who recognizes him, and he desecrates the Sabbath by uprooting a radish to prove his identity.

items.text: First debate: Acher and Rabbi Meir on opposites
items.text_en: First debate: Acher and Rabbi Meir on opposites
items.desc_en: Acher asks Rabbi Meir about the verse 'God made one opposite the other.' Rabbi Meir explains that God created opposites in nature, but Acher counters with Rabbi Akiva's teaching that God created righteous and wicked, each with two portions in Eden and Gehinnom. Rav Mesharshiya cites verses supporting this.

sub.desc_en: Acher asks Rabbi Meir about the verse 'God made one opposite the other.'
Rabbi Meir explains that God created opposites in nature, such as mountains and hills, seas and rivers.
Acher counters with Rabbi Akiva's teaching that God created righteous and wicked, each with two portions in Eden and Gehinnom.
Rav Mesharshiya cites verses supporting the idea that righteous and wicked each receive a double portion.

items.text: Second debate: Acher and Rabbi Meir on Torah's value
items.text_en: Second debate: Acher and Rabbi Meir on Torah's value
items.desc_en: Acher asks about the verse comparing Torah to gold, glass, and fine gold. Rabbi Meir explains that Torah is hard to acquire but easy to lose. Acher counters with Rabbi Akiva's teaching that even a Torah scholar who sins can be restored, like broken vessels. Acher is urged to repent but refuses, citing the heavenly voice excluding him.

sub.desc_en: Acher asks Rabbi Meir about the verse comparing Torah to gold, glass, and fine gold.
Rabbi Meir explains that Torah is hard to acquire like gold and fine gold, but easy to lose like glass.
Acher counters with Rabbi Akiva's teaching that even a Torah scholar who sins can be restored, like broken vessels.
Rabbi Meir urges Acher to repent.

sub.text: Acher's refusal citing the heavenly voice
sub.text_en: Acher's refusal citing the heavenly voice
sub.desc_en: Acher refuses to repent, citing the heavenly voice that excluded him from forgiveness.

items.text: Acher's final rejection and the children's verses
items.text_en: Acher's final rejection and the children's verses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir follows Acher on Shabbat to learn Torah, but Acher warns him about the Shabbat boundary. Rabbi Meir urges him to repent, but Acher again cites the heavenly voice. Acher then tests children in synagogues, and their verses condemn him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts that Acher rode a horse on Shabbat, and Rabbi Meir walked behind him to learn Torah; Acher warned Rabbi Meir to turn back because he had measured the Shabbat boundary.
Rabbi Meir urges Acher to repent.
Acher rejects Rabbi Meir's plea, citing the heavenly voice that excluded him from repentance.

Acher took Rabbi Meir to a synagogue and tested children with verses; the first child recited 'אין שלום אמר ה׳ לרשעים' (There is no peace for the wicked), and the second child recited 'כי אם תכבסי בנתר ותרבי לך בורית נכתם עונך לפני' (Though you wash with niter and much soap, your iniquity is marked before Me), both condemning him.

items.text: Acher's encounter with the child and the thirteen synagogues
items.text_en: Acher's encounter with the child and the thirteen synagogues
items.desc_en: Acher asks a child to recite his verse, but the child recites a verse that rebukes Acher. Acher then takes the child to thirteen synagogues, where the same verse is recited. Later, the child recites a verse about the wicked, which Acher mishears as a personal insult, leading him to tear the child with a knife or express a wish to do so.

sub.desc_en: Acher asks a child to recite his verse, and the child recites a verse that rebukes Acher.
Acher takes the child to thirteen synagogues, and in each the same verse is recited.
The child recites a verse about the wicked, which Acher mishears as a personal insult, leading him to tear the child with a knife or express a wish to do so.

items.text: Debate over Acher's judgment and the smoke from his grave
items.text_en: Debate over Acher's judgment and the smoke from his grave
items.desc_en: After Acher's death, the sages debate whether he should be judged or enter the World to Come. Rabbi Meir wishes to bring smoke from Acher's grave, and after Rabbi Meir's death, smoke rises. Rabbi Yochanan rebukes this and extinguishes the smoke after his own death, with a eulogizer praising him.

sub.desc_en: The sages debate Acher's fate after his death, concluding he should neither be judged nor enter the World to Come.
Rabbi Meir argues that Acher should be judged and then enter the World to Come, and wishes to bring smoke from his grave as a sign.
After Rabbi Meir's death, smoke rises from Acher's grave, fulfilling Rabbi Meir's wish.
Rabbi Yochanan rebukes Rabbi Meir's action, questioning whether it is proper to disgrace one's teacher and expressing inability to save Acher.
Rabbi Yochanan wishes to extinguish the smoke from Acher's grave, and after his death the smoke ceases.
A eulogizer praises Rabbi Yochanan, saying even the gatekeeper could not stand before him.

items.text: Acher's daughter seeks charity from Rabbi
items.text_en: Acher's daughter seeks charity from Rabbi
items.desc_en: Acher's daughter comes to Rabbi for sustenance. Rabbi initially refuses, citing a verse that Acher would have no descendants, but she pleads to remember his Torah, not his deeds. A fire surrounds Rabbi's seat, and he weeps, concluding that those who disgrace Torah suffer thus, so those who honor it will be rewarded even more.

sub.desc_en: Acher's daughter comes to Rabbi and identifies herself when asked.
Rabbi questions whether Acher has any descendants left, citing a verse that he would have none.
Acher's daughter pleads with Rabbi to remember Acher's Torah study, not his sinful deeds.
A fire surrounds Rabbi's seat, and he weeps, concluding that those who disgrace Torah suffer thus, so those who honor it will be rewarded even more.

items.text: Justification for Rabbi Meir learning from Acher
items.text_en: Justification for Rabbi Meir learning from Acher
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Meir could learn Torah from Acher, given the principle that a teacher must be like an angel. Resh Lakish and Rabbi Chanina provide verses to justify learning from a sinful teacher, distinguishing between a great and a small student. The contradiction between verses is resolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Meir could learn Torah from Acher, citing the principle that one should only learn from a teacher who is like an angel of God.
Resh Lakish answers that Rabbi Meir found a verse: 'Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise, and direct your heart to MY knowledge' — not to their knowledge, but to God's knowledge.

Rabbi Chanina provides another verse: 'Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house' — implying one can learn even from a sinful teacher by ignoring their personal flaws.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between the two verses: one applies to a great student (who can learn from any teacher), the other to a small student (who needs a righteous teacher).

items.text: Rava's parable of the walnut
items.text_en: Rava's parable of the walnut
items.desc_en: Rava teaches that Torah scholars are compared to a walnut: even if the shell is dirty, the inside is not spoiled. Similarly, a Torah scholar's Torah is not defiled even if he sins.

sub.desc_en: Rava teaches that Torah scholars are compared to a walnut: even if the shell is dirty, the inside is not spoiled, so a Torah scholar's Torah is not defiled even if he sins.

items.text: Elijah's report on God's acceptance of Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Elijah's report on God's acceptance of Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Sheila asks Elijah what God is doing. Elijah reports that God recites teachings from all rabbis except Rabbi Meir, because he learned from Acher. Rabba bar Sheila argues that Rabbi Meir found a pomegranate, ate the inside, and threw away the peel. God then recites a teaching from Rabbi Meir about the Shekhinah's suffering over the blood of the wicked.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Sheila finds Elijah and asks what God is doing; Elijah reports that God recites teachings from all rabbis except Rabbi Meir because he learned from Acher.
Rabba bar Sheila objects, arguing that Rabbi Meir found a pomegranate, ate the inside, and threw away the peel, so his learning from Acher should not disqualify him.
Elijah reports that God now recites a teaching from Rabbi Meir about the Shekhinah's suffering over the blood of the wicked, and by קל וחומר (a fortiori) over the blood of the righteous.

items.text: Samuel's consolation to Rav Yehuda about the sages' fate
items.text_en: Samuel's consolation to Rav Yehuda about the sages' fate
items.desc_en: Samuel finds Rav Yehuda crying over the fate of the sages, who are described as counting letters, weighing kal va'chomer, and knowing 300 laws about the flying tower. Rabbi Ami adds that Doeg and Achitophel asked 300 questions about the flying tower. Samuel consoles him that they had mud in their hearts (i.e., were wicked).

sub.desc_en: Samuel finds Rav Yehuda crying and asks him why he is crying.
Rav Yehuda laments the fate of the sages, citing the verse about the scribe, weigher, and tower-counter, and explaining that they knew 300 laws about the flying tower.
Rabbi Ami adds that Doeg and Achitophel asked 300 questions about the flying tower.
Rav Yehuda asks what will become of us (the sages) given that even such great figures have no share in the world to come.
Samuel consoles Rav Yehuda by saying that those sages had mud in their hearts (i.e., were wicked), implying that the righteous sages are not condemned.

items.text: Acher's Greek song and Nimosis's question
items.text_en: Acher's Greek song and Nimosis's question
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes Acher's constant Greek song and his books of heresy. Nimosis the Gardi asks Rabbi Meir a parable about wool that goes into a vat, and Rabbi Meir responds about those who were clean from their mother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Acher never ceased from Greek song and that heretical books fell from his bosom when he left the study hall.
Nimosis the Gardi asks Rabbi Meir a parable: does all wool that goes into a vat come out clean?
Rabbi Meir responds that only those who were clean from their mother come out, while those who were not clean do not.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's safe ascent and descent
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's safe ascent and descent
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Akiva ascended and descended in peace, and the ministering angels sought to push him, but God told them to leave him alone, as he was worthy to use His glory.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Akiva ascended and descended safely, and God protected him from the ministering angels because he was worthy to use His glory.

items.text: Homiletical interpretations of divine epithets
items.text_en: Homiletical interpretations of divine epithets
items.desc_en: Four Amoraim offer different scriptural derivations for the idea that God is uniquely distinguished among His heavenly retinue. Each cites a verse to show that God's greatness is incomparable even among the myriads of angels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what homiletical interpretation each Amora derived from the verses.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'וְאָתָא מֵרִבְבוֹת קֹדֶשׁ' to mean that God is a unique sign among His myriads.
Rabbi Avahu interprets the verse 'דָּגוּל מֵרְבָבָה' to mean that God is a distinctive example among His myriads.
Reish Lakish interprets the verse 'ה׳ צְבָאוֹת שְׁמוֹ' to mean that God is the Master over His heavenly host.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan cites the verses from the revelation to Elijah to show that God is found in the still small voice, not in the wind, earthquake, or fire.

items.text: Six traits of demons
items.text_en: Six traits of demons
items.desc_en: A Tannaic tradition enumerates six characteristics of demons: three like ministering angels (wings, flight, knowledge of the future) and three like humans (eating, procreation, death). The Gemara clarifies that their knowledge comes from overhearing behind the curtain.

sub.desc_en: The Tannaic tradition enumerates six traits of demons: three like ministering angels (wings, flight, knowledge of the future) and three like humans.
The Gemara objects: can it enter your mind that demons truly know the future?
The Gemara resolves: rather, they overhear from behind the curtain (פרגוד), like ministering angels.
The tradition concludes the three human-like traits: eating, procreation, and death.

items.text: Six traits of humans
items.text_en: Six traits of humans
items.desc_en: A parallel tradition lists six characteristics of humans: three like ministering angels (intellect, upright posture, Hebrew speech) and three like animals (eating, procreation, elimination).

sub.desc_en: The Tanna lists six traits of humans: three like ministering angels (intellect, upright posture, Hebrew speech) and three like animals (eating, procreation, elimination).

items.text: The prohibition against speculating about what is before
items.text_en: The prohibition against speculating about what is before
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's warning against looking into 'what is before' (the future), since it has not yet happened. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar answer with a parable: a king who built a palace on a garbage dump does not want the dump mentioned, so too God created the world from chaos and does not want that mentioned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's inclusion of 'what is before' (the future) among forbidden speculations, since the future has not yet happened.

Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar answer with a parable: a king who built a palace on a garbage dump does not want the dump mentioned, so too God created the world from chaos and does not want that mentioned.

items.text: One who does not respect God's honor
items.text_en: One who does not respect God's honor
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies two types of people who fail to respect God's honor: one who gazes at the rainbow (which resembles the divine glory) and one who sins in secret. A contradiction is raised from Rabbi Ila'a who advises sinning in private to avoid public desecration; the resolution distinguishes between one who can overcome his inclination and one who cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general statement: one who does not respect God's honor would be better off not having been born.
The Gemara asks: what specific behavior does this refer to?
Rabbi Abba answers: it is one who gazes at the rainbow, citing the verse that compares the rainbow to the appearance of God's glory.
Rav Yosef answers: it is one who sins in secret, citing Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching that such a person pushes aside the feet of the Shekhinah.
The Gemara objects: but Rabbi Ila'a the Elder said that if one's evil inclination overcomes him, he should sin in private to avoid public desecration of God's name.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the case of one who can overcome his inclination is different from the case of one who cannot.

items.text: Three things that dim one's eyesight
items.text_en: Three things that dim one's eyesight
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Nachmani teaches that looking at three things dims the eyes: the rainbow, the Nasi, and the priests when they bless Israel with the explicit name.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Nachmani teaches that looking at three things dims one's eyesight: the rainbow, the Nasi, and the priests when they bless Israel with the explicit name.

items.text: Witnesses against sin
items.text_en: Witnesses against sin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Nachmani expounds that one should not believe the evil inclination's promise that God will forgive. Various opinions are given about who testifies against a person: the stones of his house, his soul, two ministering angels, or his limbs.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Nachmani expounds the verse 'אל תאמינו ברע' to warn against believing the evil inclination's promise that God will forgive sin.
The Gemara raises the question: who will testify against a person for his sins?
One opinion answers that the stones and beams of a person's house testify against him, citing the verse 'כי אבן מקיר תזעק'.
The Sages say that a person's soul testifies against him, interpreting the verse 'משוכבת חיקך שמור פתחי פיך'.
Rabbi Zerika says that the two ministering angels who accompany a person testify against him, citing the verse 'כי מלאכיו יצוה לך'.
The Sages (another opinion) say that a person's limbs testify against him, citing the verse 'ואתם עדי נאום ה' ואני אל'.

items.text: Mishnah: The dispute over semikhah
items.text_en: Mishnah: The dispute over semikhah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records the alternating opinions of the zugot (pairs) regarding whether one may perform semikhah (laying of hands) on a festival offering. The pattern continues until Hillel and Shammai, with Menachem exiting and Shammai entering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the alternating opinions of the zugot (pairs) regarding whether one may perform semikhah (laying of hands) on a festival offering, concluding with Hillel permitting and Shammai forbidding.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Baraita on the Zugot
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Baraita on the Zugot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the first pairs were Nesi'im and their seconds were Avot Beit Din. The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute the specific roles of Yehudah ben Tabai and Shimon ben Shatach.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the first pairs were Nesi'im and their seconds were Avot Beit Din.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute the specific roles of Yehudah ben Tabai and Shimon ben Shatach.

items.text: Story of Yehudah ben Tabai and Shimon ben Shatach
items.text_en: Story of Yehudah ben Tabai and Shimon ben Shatach
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Yehudah ben Tabai killed a false witness to uproot Sadducee beliefs, but Shimon ben Shatach rebuked him for shedding innocent blood. Yehudah ben Tabai accepted not to rule halakhah without Shimon ben Shatach, and mourned at the victim's grave.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who taught the baraita about Yehudah ben Tabai killing a false witness to uproot Sadducee beliefs.
Shimon ben Shatach rebukes Yehudah ben Tabai for shedding innocent blood, citing the halakhah that false witnesses are executed only when both are disqualified.
Yehudah ben Tabai immediately accepted not to rule halakhah without Shimon ben Shatach.
The Gemara recounts that Yehudah ben Tabai mourned at the victim's grave, and his voice was heard until he died, proving it was his own voice.

items.text: Analysis of the Story and the Roles of Nasi and Av Beit Din
items.text_en: Analysis of the Story and the Roles of Nasi and Av Beit Din
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava questions the story, and the Gemara analyzes it according to the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about who was Nasi and who was Av Beit Din. It concludes that Yehudah ben Tabai's acceptance meant he would not even join Shimon ben Shatach in a ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi whether Yehudah ben Tabai might have appeased the executed witness or sued him in court, rather than admitting error.

The Gemara analyzes the story according to the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages, showing that only if Yehudah ben Tabai was Nasi (per Rabbi Meir) could he have ruled in Shimon ben Shatach's presence, but if he was Av Beit Din (per the Sages), he would not have ruled in the Nasi's presence.
The Gemara resolves that Yehudah ben Tabai's acceptance meant he would not even join Shimon ben Shatach in a ruling, not that he ruled independently.

items.text: Departure of Menahem and Entry of Shammai
items.text_en: Departure of Menahem and Entry of Shammai
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses where Menahem went: Abaye says he went to evil culture, Rava says he went to the king's service, and a baraita supports Rava's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where Menahem went after departing from the zugot (pairs).
Abaye answers that Menahem went to evil culture (heresy).
Rava answers that Menahem went to the king's service (royal court).
A baraita supports Rava's view, stating that Menahem went to the king's service accompanied by eighty pairs of students dressed in silk garments.

items.text: Rav Yochanan on the Severity of Shevut
items.text_en: Rav Yochanan on the Severity of Shevut
items.desc_en: Rav Yochanan states that one should never consider shevut (rabbinic rest) light, as semikhah is only a shevut and great sages disputed it. The Gemara clarifies that the dispute was specifically about shevut, not about semikhah itself.

sub.text: Rav Shemen bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Shemen bar Abba reports Rabbi Yochanan's statement that one should never consider shevut (rabbinic rest) light, because semikhah (leaning on the sacrifice) is only a shevut, yet great sages disputed it.
The Gemara asks: Is this obvious? It must be that Rabbi Yochanan needed to teach about shevut of a mitzvah (rabbinic rest related to a commandment).

The Gemara answers that this too is obvious, but Rabbi Yochanan's statement comes to exclude the view that the dispute was about semikhah itself; rather, it teaches that the dispute was specifically about shevut.

items.text: Dispute over Whether Semikhah Requires Full Force
items.text_en: Dispute over Whether Semikhah Requires Full Force
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama deduces that semikhah requires full force. The Gemara challenges this from a baraita about women semikhah, and Rabbi Ami explains that the case was not valid semikhah but only to please the women.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama deduces from the dispute over semikhah that it requires full force (בכל כוחו), arguing that if it did not, what would be the issue with performing it?

The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that cites the verse 'דבר אל בני ישראל... וסמך' (Speak to the children of Israel... and he shall lean), which is interpreted to exclude women from obligatory semikhah, but Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yishmael permit women to perform semikhah voluntarily.

Rabbi Yosei recounts a story where women performed semikhah on a peace-offering calf in the Women's Courtyard, and Abba Elazar explains it was only to please the women, not valid semikhah; the Gemara argues that if semikhah required full force, this would be a forbidden act of service with consecrated animals, concluding that semikhah does not require full force.

The Gemara defends Rami bar Chama's position by suggesting that the women were told to press their hands lightly (אקפו ידייכו), but then objects that if so, the explanation 'not because semikhah applies to women' would be redundant, as it would already be clear that it is not valid semikhah at all.

Rabbi Ami resolves the difficulty by explaining that Abba Elazar's statement contains two points: first, that the women's action was not valid semikhah at all, and second, that it was done only to please the women.

items.text: Rav Papa's Deduction about Tzidadin
items.text_en: Rav Papa's Deduction about Tzidadin
items.desc_en: Rav Papa deduces from the previous discussion that tzidadin (sides) are forbidden, as otherwise one could perform semikhah on the side.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa deduces from the previous discussion that tzidadin (sides) are forbidden, as otherwise one could perform semikhah on the side.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that even if one permits צדדין, whatever is attached to the animal is considered like the animal itself, resolving a previous difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by asserting that even if one permits צדדין (the sides), anything attached to the animal is considered like the animal itself.

items.text: Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on festival offerings
items.text_en: Mishnah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on festival offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records the dispute: Beit Shammai permits bringing peace-offerings but not burnt-offerings on a festival, and forbids semikhah; Beit Hillel permits both. It also discusses the 'day of slaughter' for Shavuot when it falls on Shabbat or Friday, and rules that the High Priest does not wear his vestments, and mourning and fasting are permitted.

sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai rules that on a festival one may bring peace-offerings but not burnt-offerings, and may not perform semikhah.
Beit Hillel permits bringing both peace-offerings and burnt-offerings on a festival, and also permits semikhah.
The Mishnah records the dispute about the 'day of slaughter' for Shavuot when it falls on Friday: Beit Shammai says it is after Shabbat, Beit Hillel says there is no such day.
Both schools agree that if Shavuot falls on Shabbat, the day of slaughter is after Shabbat.

sub.text: Mishnah: High Priest's vestments and mourning
sub.text_en: Mishnah: High Priest's vestments and mourning
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that the High Priest does not wear his vestments on Shavuot, and mourning and fasting are permitted, to counter those who say Shavuot always falls after Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of make-up days for Shavuot
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of make-up days for Shavuot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya derives that Shavuot has make-up days for seven days, by analogy to Pesach, based on the verse grouping the three festivals.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya derives that Shavuot has make-up days for seven days, by analogy to Pesach, based on the verse grouping the three festivals.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the analogy to Sukkot
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the analogy to Sukkot
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not analogize Shavuot to Sukkot, which has eight days? It answers that the eighth day is a separate festival, but only for matters of פָּזֵ״ר קֶשֶׁ״ב; for make-up days, it is a completion of the first. The principle 'if you grasp too much you grasp nothing' is invoked.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not analogize Shavuot to Sukkot, which has eight days for make-up offerings?
The Gemara answers that the eighth day of Sukkot is a separate festival, but only for matters of פָּזֵ״ר קֶשֶׁ״ב; for make-up days, it is a completion of the first.
The Gemara invokes the principle 'if you grasp too much you grasp nothing; if you grasp a little you grasp it' to justify choosing the shorter analogy (seven days) over the longer one (eight days).

items.text: Alternative purpose of the analogy to Sukkot
items.text_en: Alternative purpose of the analogy to Sukkot
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the verse writes 'Sukkot' to analogize it to Pesach for the law of lodging overnight, and then asks from where that law is derived for Pesach itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for what halachic purpose the Torah wrote 'Sukkot' in the verse, and answers that it is to analogize Sukkot to Pesach for the law of lodging overnight (לִינָה).
The Gemara then asks from where the law of lodging overnight is derived for Pesach itself.

items.text: Opening verse citation
items.text_en: Opening verse citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse (Deuteronomy 16:7) to introduce the concept of turning back in the morning, which may relate to the make-up period for festivals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'וּפָנִיתָ בַבֹּקֶר וְהָלַכְתָּ לְאֹהָלֶיךָ' (Deuteronomy 16:7) to introduce the concept of turning back in the morning.

items.text: Mishnah on Shavuot's make-up day and the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Mishnah on Shavuot's make-up day and the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes a Mishnah about Shavuot falling on Shabbat eve: Beit Shammai says there is a make-up day after Shabbat, Beit Hillel says there is no make-up day. The Gemara clarifies that Beit Hillel means no need for a make-up day, not that there is none at all, and explains why both cases (this and the earlier dispute about bringing offerings) are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when Shavuot falls on Shabbat eve, Beit Shammai says there is a make-up day after Shabbat, while Beit Hillel says there is no make-up day.
The Gemara asks whether Beit Hillel means there is absolutely no make-up day.
The Gemara answers that Beit Hillel means it does not need a make-up day, not that there is none at all.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to teach this, since the same dispute was already presented in an earlier Mishnah about bringing offerings.
The Gemara cites the earlier Mishnah where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute about bringing peace-offerings and burnt-offerings on Shavuot.
The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: each one prevents a potential inference from the other, so the Mishnah must teach both disputes.

items.text: Attempt to prove make-up period from a baraita
items.text_en: Attempt to prove make-up period from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita stating that one who did not celebrate on Passover's seven days, Sukkot's eight days, and Shavuot's first day cannot celebrate later. It initially assumes this refers to Shavuot's Yom Tov, but corrects it to mean the make-up day, and then attempts to prove that the make-up period is only one day, but the text says 'days of make-up' implying multiple days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing the festivals one must celebrate on their appointed days, implying that Shavuot has only one day for celebration.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita's reference to 'the first day of Shavuot' means the actual Yom Tov day.
The Gemara corrects that the baraita refers to the make-up day (יום טבוח), not the Yom Tov itself.
The Gemara attempts to prove from the baraita that the make-up period is only one day.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita actually says 'days of make-up' (plural), implying multiple days, not just one.

items.text: Rabbah bar Shmuel's teaching and Rava's objection
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Shmuel's teaching and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Shmuel teaches that just as the month is sanctified by counting days, so too Shavuot is sanctified by counting days, implying one day. Rava objects, noting that we count both days and weeks for Shavuot, citing Abaye's statement about the mitzvah to count days and weeks, and the verse 'Chag Shavuot'.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbah bar Shmuel's teaching
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbah bar Shmuel's teaching
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbah bar Shmuel's teaching that just as the month is sanctified by counting its days, so too Shavuot is sanctified by counting its days, implying it is only one day.
Rava objects, arguing that we count both days and weeks for Shavuot, citing Abaye's statement about the mitzvah to count days and weeks, and the verse 'Chag Shavuot'.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teaching on Shavuot's make-up
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teaching on Shavuot's make-up
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches from the verse 'וּקְרָאתֶם וּבְקֻצְרְכֶם' that Shavuot is a holiday where one may call (i.e., bring offerings) and reap, implying make-up days are permitted for reaping, which is forbidden on Yom Tov itself, thus proving the make-up period is not Yom Tov.

sub.text: School of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: School of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches from the verse 'וּקְרָאתֶם וּבְקֻצְרְכֶם' that Shavuot is the holiday where one may call (bring offerings) and reap.
The Gemara asks: When is this permitted? If on Yom Tov itself, is reaping on Yom Tov permitted?
The Gemara concludes: Rather, it must refer to the make-up days (תשלומין), proving they are not Yom Tov and thus permit reaping.

items.text: Need for both Rabbi Elazar-Oshaya and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teachings
items.text_en: Need for both Rabbi Elazar-Oshaya and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teachings
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teaching are necessary: without the latter, one might think Shavuot's make-up days are forbidden in labor like Passover's make-up; without the former, one might think Shavuot's make-up is entirely permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teaching are necessary: without the latter, one might think Shavuot's make-up days are forbidden in labor like Passover's make-up; without the former, one might think Shavuot's make-up is entirely permitted.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Elazar's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Elazar's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Elazar's statement about not knowing the exact number of days was taught by Rabbi Oshaya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Elazar's statement about not knowing the exact number of days was taught by Rabbi Oshaya.

items.text: Resh Lakish's derivation from 'Chag HaKatzir'
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's derivation from 'Chag HaKatzir'
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish argues that the verse 'Chag HaKatzir' refers to Shavuot, and since harvesting is forbidden on Yom Tov, it must refer to the make-up period (tashlumin).

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish interprets the verse 'וְחַג הַקָּצִיר' (the harvest festival) to refer to Shavuot (עֲצֶרֶת), the festival during which one harvests.
The Gemara questions whether the harvest mentioned in the verse could occur on the festival day itself, since harvesting is forbidden on יוֹם טוֹב (a festival day).
The Gemara concludes that the verse must refer to the make-up period (תַּשְׁלוּמִין) for the festival offering, not the festival day itself.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's counter-argument from 'Chag HaAsif'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's counter-argument from 'Chag HaAsif'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Resh Lakish by comparing to 'Chag HaAsif' (Sukkot), which cannot refer to Yom Tov or Chol HaMoed due to labor prohibitions, but rather to the season of gathering. Similarly, 'Chag HaKatzir' refers to the season of harvest.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects by applying the same logic to the verse 'חַג הָאָסִיף' (the ingathering festival), which would similarly refer to Sukkot.
Rabbi Yochanan questions whether the ingathering could occur on the festival day itself, since work is forbidden on יוֹם טוֹב.
Rabbi Yochanan then questions whether the ingathering could occur on חוֹל הַמּוֹעֵד (the intermediate festival days), since work is also forbidden then.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the verse refers to the festival that comes at the time of ingathering, not the act of ingathering itself, and similarly for Shavuot.

items.text: Implication that both agree Chol HaMoed is forbidden in labor
items.text_en: Implication that both agree Chol HaMoed is forbidden in labor
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that both Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan assume that Chol HaMoed is forbidden in labor, as otherwise their arguments would not hold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that both Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan agree that work is forbidden on חוֹל הַמּוֹעֵד (the intermediate festival days).

items.text: First baraita: Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan on the source
items.text_en: First baraita: Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan on the source
items.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi Yoshiya deriving the prohibition from the verse 'Et Chag HaMatzot Tishmor', while Rabbi Yonatan uses a kal vachomer. The Gemara then raises and refutes objections to the kal vachomer, ultimately supporting it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the prohibition of work on חול המועד (intermediate festival days).
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yoshiya derives the prohibition from the verse 'אֶת חַג הַמַּצּוֹת תִּשְׁמוֹר' (You shall keep the festival of matzot), teaching that חול המועד is forbidden in work.

Rabbi Yonatan argues that no verse is needed, using a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if the first and seventh days of the festival, which have no sanctity before or after them, are forbidden in work, then חול המועד, which has sanctity before and after, should certainly be forbidden.
An objection is raised: the six days of Creation have sanctity before and after (Shabbat), yet work is permitted on them, undermining the קל וחומר.
The objection is rejected: the six days of Creation have no מוסף (additional festival offering), unlike חול המועד which does.
A second objection is raised: ראש חודש (the new month) has a מוסף offering yet work is permitted on it.
The objection is rejected: ראש חודש is not called 'מִקְרָא קֹדֶשׁ' (a holy convocation), unlike חול המועד which is, so the קל וחומר stands.

items.text: Second baraita: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Second baraita: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Another baraita has Rabbi Yosei HaGelili deriving the prohibition from 'Kol Melechet Avoda Lo Ta'asu', while Rabbi Akiva derives it from the verse 'Eileh Moadei Hashem', arguing that the term 'Shabbaton' applies to Chol HaMoed.

sub.desc_en: Another baraita cites Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who derives from the verse 'כָּל מְלֶאכֶת עֲבוֹדָה לֹא תַעֲשׂוּ' that work is forbidden on חוֹל הַמּוֹעֵד.

Rabbi Akiva argues that the prohibition is derived from the verse 'אֵלֶּה מוֹעֲדֵי ה, which mentions 'שַׁבָּתוֹן' (rest) only for the first and seventh days, implying that the intermediate days are also forbidden for work.

items.text: Third baraita: Derivation from 'Sheishet Yamim Tochal Matzot'
items.text_en: Third baraita: Derivation from 'Sheishet Yamim Tochal Matzot'
items.desc_en: A third baraita derives the prohibition from the verse 'Sheishet Yamim Tochal Matzot', comparing the six days to the seventh, but concludes that the prohibition is not absolute and is left to the Sages to determine which days and which labors are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'Sheishet Yamim Tochal Matzot' and proposes a comparison: just as the seventh day is restricted from all labor, so too the six days should be restricted from all labor.
The baraita rejects the initial comparison by citing the continuation of the verse, which specifies that only the seventh day is restricted from all labor, not the six days.
The baraita concludes that the verse does not specify which days or labors are forbidden, but leaves this determination to the Sages.

items.text: Discussion on eulogies and fasts on Chol HaMoed
items.text_en: Discussion on eulogies and fasts on Chol HaMoed
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses that eulogies and fasts are permitted on Chol HaMoed, contrary to those who place Shavuot after Shabbat. It recounts an incident where Rabbi Tarfon prevented eulogies for Aleksa because it was a Yom Tov, and resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing between Yom Tov after Shabbat and Yom Tov on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that eulogies and fasts are permitted on Chol HaMoed, contradicting those who place Shavuot after Shabbat.
The Gemara recounts an incident where Rabbi Tarfon prevented eulogies for Aleksa because it was a Yom Tov of Shavuot.
The Gemara objects that it cannot be a Yom Tov (since people would not come for a eulogy), and suggests it was a day of slaughter (יום טבוח).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a Yom Tov that falls after Shabbat (where eulogies are forbidden) and a Yom Tov that falls on Shabbat (where eulogies are permitted).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Hierarchy of Hand Purification
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Hierarchy of Hand Purification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah outlines the levels of hand purification: netilah (pouring) for chullin, ma'aser, and terumah; tevilah (immersion) for kodashim; and for chatat, hand impurity affects the body. It then details the rule that one who immerses for a higher level is restricted for a lower one, and the status of garments as midras for successive levels of sanctity, with examples of pious individuals.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the hierarchy of hand purification: netilah (pouring) for chullin, ma'aser, and terumah; tevilah (immersion) for kodashim; and for chatat, hand impurity affects the body.
The Mishnah details the rule that one who immerses for a higher level is restricted for a lower one, and that immersion without intention is as if not immersed.
The Mishnah states the status of garments as midras for successive levels of sanctity.
The Mishnah provides examples of pious individuals: Yosef ben Yoezer and Yochanan ben Gudgda, whose garments were considered midras for higher levels of sanctity.

items.text: Gemara's Challenge: Do Chullin and Ma'aser Require Hand Washing?
items.text_en: Gemara's Challenge: Do Chullin and Ma'aser Require Hand Washing?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether chullin and ma'aser require netilat yadayim, citing a baraita that lists terumah and bikurim as requiring hand washing, but not ma'aser, and certainly not chullin. This creates an apparent contradiction with the Mishnah's inclusion of ma'aser and chullin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether non-sacred food and tithes require hand washing.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that lists terumah and bikurim as requiring hand washing, but not ma'aser, and certainly not chullin.
The Gemara states that the contradiction applies both to ma'aser and to chullin.

items.text: First Resolution: Rabbi Meir vs. Sages on Ma'aser
items.text_en: First Resolution: Rabbi Meir vs. Sages on Ma'aser
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding ma'aser by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Meir, who holds that ma'aser requires hand washing, and the baraita to the Sages, who prohibit eating ma'aser without washing. However, the contradiction regarding chullin remains.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction regarding ma'aser by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Meir and the baraita to the Sages.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir permits chullin and ma'aser after hand washing, while the Sages prohibit ma'aser.
The Gemara notes that the contradiction regarding chullin remains unresolved.

items.text: Second Resolution: Eating vs. Touching, and Rav Shimi's Objection
items.text_en: Second Resolution: Eating vs. Touching, and Rav Shimi's Objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially distinguishes between eating (which requires washing) and touching (which does not) to resolve the chullin contradiction. Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects, arguing that the Sages only dispute Rabbi Meir regarding eating ma'aser, not touching ma'aser or eating chullin. The Gemara then distinguishes between eating bread (requires washing) and eating fruit (does not), citing Rav Nachman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between eating (requires hand-washing) and touching (does not).

Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects that the Sages only dispute Rabbi Meir regarding eating ma'aser, not touching ma'aser or eating chullin, so the distinction between eating and touching does not resolve the chullin contradiction.

sub.text: Gemara's revised resolution citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Gemara's revised resolution citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: The Gemara revises the resolution: both cases involve eating, but one is eating bread (requires hand-washing) and the other is eating fruit (does not), citing Rav Nachman's statement that one who washes hands for fruit is arrogant.

items.text: Baraita on Intention for Hand Washing
items.text_en: Baraita on Intention for Hand Washing
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that for hand washing, intention is required for purity; without intention, hands remain impure. Another baraita contradicts this, stating that intention is irrelevant. Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by applying the first baraita to chullin and the second to terumah.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that for hand washing, intent is required for purity; without intent, hands remain impure.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita that says intent is irrelevant for hand washing.
Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between chullin (where intent is not required) and terumah (where intent is required).
Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction: the first baraita applies to chullin (non-sacred food), and the second baraita applies to terumah (priestly portion).

items.text: Proof that חולין do not require intention
items.text_en: Proof that חולין do not require intention
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah about a wave with 40 se'ah falling on a person and vessels, implying that vessels (which lack intention) become pure, and by analogy, a person without intention also becomes pure. This supports the claim that for חולין, intention is not required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a proof that חולין (non-sacred food) do not require intention, citing a Mishnah about a wave with 40 se'ah falling on a person and vessels, implying that vessels (which lack intention) become pure, and by analogy, a person without intention also becomes pure.

items.text: Rejection and resolution of the proof
items.text_en: Rejection and resolution of the proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the proof, suggesting the case might involve a person sitting and waiting for the wave, implying intention. It then explains that the Mishnah's purpose is to teach that we do not decree against such cases due to concerns about using rainwater pools or waves (כיפּין).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the proof from the Mishnah of the wave, suggesting that the case might involve a person sitting and waiting for the wave, implying intention, and that the analogy to vessels would then require intention for vessels as well.
The Gemara asks: if the case involves a person sitting and waiting, what novel teaching does the Mishnah convey?
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah teaches that we do not decree a prohibition against using such waves due to concerns about using rainwater pools or detached waves (כיפּין).

items.text: Source that one does not immerse in waves (כיפּין)
items.text_en: Source that one does not immerse in waves (כיפּין)
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that one may immerse in the heads of waves (ראשין) but not in the hollows (כיפּין), because immersion cannot be in the air.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that one immerses in the heads of waves (ראשין) but not in the hollows (כיפּין), because immersion cannot be in the air.

items.text: Alternative proof from Mishnah about fruits and intention
items.text_en: Alternative proof from Mishnah about fruits and intention
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah about fruits falling into a water channel: if one with impure hands reaches in to take them, his hands are pure but the fruits are not susceptible to impurity (unless he intended to wash his hands). This shows that for חולין, intention is not required for purification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about fruits in a water channel to prove that for חולין (non-sacred food), intention is not required for purification.

items.text: Rabbah's objection and resolution regarding intention for מעשר
items.text_en: Rabbah's objection and resolution regarding intention for מעשר
items.desc_en: Rabbah objects to Rav Nachman from a baraita: one who immersed for חולין and was designated for חולין is forbidden for מעשר, implying that without designation, immersion is invalid. Rav Nachman explains that the baraita means even if designated, it is still forbidden for מעשר. Another objection about one who immersed without designation is resolved by distinguishing between חולין and מעשר.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah objects to Rav Nachman from a baraita: one who immersed for חולין and was designated for חולין is forbidden for מעשר, implying that without designation, immersion is invalid.
Rav Nachman explains that the baraita means even if designated, it is still forbidden for מעשר.
The Gemara objects with another baraita: one who immersed without designation is as if he did not immerse at all, implying total invalidity.

The Gemara resolves: the baraita means as if he did not immerse for מעשר, but he did immerse for חולין, and a supporting baraita confirms that one who immersed without designation is forbidden for מעשר but permitted for חולין.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's ruling and objection about one who immersed and ascended
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's ruling and objection about one who immersed and ascended
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that one who immersed and ascended may designate himself for any level he wishes. An objection is raised from a baraita: while still in the water, if designated for a light matter, he can designate for a severe matter; but after ascending, he cannot. The Gemara resolves that the baraita means that after ascending, if not designated, he can still designate; if designated, he cannot.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that one who immersed and ascended may designate himself for any level he wishes.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: while still in the water, if designated for a light matter, he can designate for a severe matter; but after ascending, he cannot designate at all.
The Gemara asks: does the baraita mean that after ascending he cannot designate at all, contradicting Rabbi Elazar?
The Gemara resolves: the baraita means that while still in the water, even if designated, he can designate; after ascending, if not designated, he can designate, but if already designated, he cannot.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the baraita and Rav Nachman's dispute
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the baraita and Rav Nachman's dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Pedat identifies the baraita as Rabbi Yehuda's view, based on a Mishnah about a mikveh with exactly 40 se'ah where two immerse sequentially. Rav Nachman bar Avuha explains that the dispute (between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages) applies only to Rabbinic elevations (מעלות דרבנן), but for actual impurity, all agree the second is impure. An alternative version reverses the ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna of the baraita that discusses one who still has one foot in the water.
Rabbi Pedat identifies the baraita as reflecting Rabbi Yehuda's view, citing a Mishnah about a mikveh with exactly 40 se'ah where two immerse sequentially.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda rules that if the first person's feet still touch the water, the second is also pure.

Rav Nachman bar Avuha explains that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages applies only to Rabbinic elevations (מעלות דרבנן), but for actual impurity, all agree the second is impure, and this aligns with Rabbi Pedat's identification.
An alternative version reverses the ruling: the dispute applies to actual impurity, but for Rabbinic elevations, all agree the second is pure, contradicting Rabbi Pedat.

items.text: Ulla's inquiry about Rabbi Yehuda's principle of גוד אחית and גוד אסיק
items.text_en: Ulla's inquiry about Rabbi Yehuda's principle of גוד אחית and גוד אסיק
items.desc_en: Ulla asks Rabbi Yochanan whether Rabbi Yehuda holds the principle of גוד אחית (extend downward) but not גוד אסיק (extend upward), or both. Rabbi Yochanan responds by citing a Mishnah about three pools in a stream where Rabbi Yehuda (citing Rabbi Meir) allows immersion in the upper pool, implying that he holds גוד אסיק as well.

sub.desc_en: Ulla asks Rabbi Yochanan whether Rabbi Yehuda holds the principle of גוד אחית (extend downward) but not גוד אסיק (extend upward), or both, regarding immersing needles in the head of the first person.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's answer citing a Mishnah
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's answer citing a Mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan responds by citing a Mishnah about three pools in a stream where Rabbi Yehuda (citing Rabbi Meir) allows immersion in the upper pool, implying that he holds גוד אסיק (extend upward) as well.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's objection and the response
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's objection and the response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir objects to the earlier statement about immersing in the upper pool, and the Gemara reports that he was told 'If it is taught, it is taught' — implying the tradition stands.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir objects to the earlier statement, asserting that immersion should be in the lower pool, not the upper one.
The Gemara reports that Rabbi Meir was told 'If it is taught, it is taught' — implying the tradition stands and the objection is dismissed.

items.text: Identifying the Mishnah's author as the Rabbis
items.text_en: Identifying the Mishnah's author as the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling about one who immerses for Chullin is in accordance with the Rabbis, who distinguish between Chullin and Ma'aser.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's ruling about one who immerses for חולין (non-sacred food) is in accordance with the Rabbis, who distinguish between חולין and מעשר (tithe).

items.text: Contradiction from the latter clause
items.text_en: Contradiction from the latter clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara points out that the latter clause of the Mishnah, regarding the garments of an am ha'aretz, aligns with Rabbi Meir's view that Chullin and Ma'aser are equivalent. This creates a contradiction: the first clause follows the Rabbis, the latter follows Rabbi Meir. The Gemara resolves this by stating that indeed the Mishnah is split between two opinions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out that the latter clause of the Mishnah, regarding the garments of an am ha'aretz being a midras for a perush and the garments of a perush being a midras for those who eat terumah, aligns with Rabbi Meir's view that Chullin and Ma'aser are equivalent.
The Gemara objects that this creates a contradiction: the first clause follows the Rabbis, but the latter clause follows Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that indeed the Mishnah is split between two opinions: the first clause follows the Rabbis and the latter clause follows Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Alternative version: five levels
items.text_en: Alternative version: five levels
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Adda teaches the latter clause as referring to five levels of sanctity, and thereby explains the entire Mishnah according to the Rabbis.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Adda's alternative version
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Adda's alternative version
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Adda teaches the latter clause of the Mishnah as referring to five levels of sanctity, thereby resolving the contradiction by interpreting the entire Mishnah according to the Rabbis.

items.text: Inference regarding Chullin prepared with Kodshim purity
items.text_en: Inference regarding Chullin prepared with Kodshim purity
items.desc_en: Rav Mari infers from the Mishnah that Chullin prepared with the purity of Kodshim is considered like Kodshim itself. The Gemara then begins to question the source of this inference.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari infers from the Mishnah that חולין (non-sacred food) prepared with the purity of קודש (sacred food) is considered like קודש itself.
The Gemara asks: from where does Rav Mari derive this inference?

items.text: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah's omission
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah's omission
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah did not list a מעלה (stringency) for certain items, and suggests it might be because they are already covered by the categories of תרומה or חולין. It cites a Tosefta where Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok argues that חולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש are like תרומה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not list a מעלה (stringency) for certain items.

The Gemara suggests that the omission is because these items are already covered by the categories of תרומה or חולין, and cites a Tosefta where Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok argues that חולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש are like תרומה.

items.text: Proof from Yosei ben Yoezer and Yochanan ben Gudgada
items.text_en: Proof from Yosei ben Yoezer and Yochanan ben Gudgada
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from the case of Yosei ben Yoezer, whose cloak was a midras for קודש, and Yochanan ben Gudgada, whose cloak was a midras for חטאת but not for קודש. This shows that Yochanan held that חולין שנעשו על טהרת קודש are like קודש.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Yosei ben Yoezer
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Yosei ben Yoezer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites that Yosei ben Yoezer's cloak was a midras for קודש (sacred food).

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Yochanan ben Gudgada
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Yochanan ben Gudgada
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites that Yochanan ben Gudgada's cloak was a midras for חטאת (sin-offering) but not for קודש.
